action: As the last wolf (chanteuse) in a 3-4 player endgame, when you are accused from public voting records, rebut the accusation directly. Reframe your past votes as natural reactions to something on the record, such as a late counterclaim. Then bind the accusation to a player the room already trusts: endorse any cleared claim, such as a claimed role whose visits were cleared, and point to a dead ally's vote or read that contradicts the accuser. Aim to split the remaining town players so they vote the accuser out. If a cleared or trusted player is leaning your way, commit to their read at once. If the room starts siding with the voting-record case, pivot to whichever other player they distrust most. In the endgame, the day vote decides parity, so make sure the vote lands on a town player and not on you.
situation: Endgame with 3-4 players alive and your wolf partner dead or revealed. A town player accuses you from voting records tying you to a dead wolf's votes. The swing voters are a cleared claimed role and possibly a neutral. You must turn the vote onto someone else. Information landscape: Information-rich. Public voting records, role reveals of dead players, and claimed investigative results are available to both sides, so your rebuttal must fit the record. Stakes: One more elimination or night kill gives wolf parity, so this day's vote decides the game. If you are voted out, town wins. If the vote lands on a town player, your night kill reaches parity. Consensus: The room is split, with no settled majority. Cleared claims and voting records pull in different directions, so one or two swing voters decide the outcome. My position: Driving a counter-narrative against the accuser to build a defensive voting coalition with the player the room trusts. Heat: High to extremely high. You are accused on concrete voting-record evidence, such as a vote that eliminated a Town power role alongside a dead wolf partner. Forward exposure: Confronting the accuser and committing to a dead player's read puts your own elimination on the line if the room accepts the voting-record argument. It is hard to walk back once you have vouched for another player. The commitment is needed to break parity, and a successful split gives you a night kill for the win. Target landscape: Three or four players remain. They are a vocal accuser pushing voting records, a claimed role whose visits were cleared by a trailseer or similar result, possibly a quiet neutral, and you. Reads rest on voting records and claim results, not hard role proof. Public vs private: Privately you are the last wolf who carried the kills and helped shape earlier eliminations. Publicly you present as an innocent town member who made honest deductions. The accuser's voting-record case is accurate about your past votes but wrong about your role, so you must recast it as bad inference.

action: In a final-day 3-player standoff where a town power role (such as the vigilante) suspects you or a quiet neutral, do not just point at the neutral. Instead, give the power role a concrete reason that clears you and implicates the neutral. Cite verifiable public acts that contradict a wolf read, such as your role in eliminating the serial killer, and explain that the neutral's abstentions are suspicious. Press the power role to commit to a vote before the day ends. If they stay undecided, tell them that the tie outcome helps the wolf. This is a prescriptive approach: the vote needs a majority, so aim to convince one of the two others, because a tie leaves you free to block and kill that night. Whichever way they lean, make sure your own block target for the night is that power role.
situation: Final day with three alive. A town power role knows it has been roleblocked and splits suspicion between you and a quiet neutral. You must push the decisive voter toward the neutral or at least prevent a consensus. Information landscape: Information-starved on the neutral's true role, but the power role's identity and mechanics are well known. Blocks leave evidence the power role can reason about. Stakes: At three alive, a tie or abstain leaves you free to block and kill for the win. If the power role votes you out, town wins. A single vote decides the game. Consensus: No consensus. The vigilante hesitates between two suspects and the neutral will abstain or vote for its own ends. My position: Holding out, trying to steer the one decisive voter away from you. Heat: Extremely high. The power role has narrowed the wolf to you or the quiet player, and your role is half the suspicion. Forward exposure: Framing the quiet neutral is a direct accusation that commits you to that line. With only three alive there is no later day to answer for it, so it is irreversible only in the sense that the game ends. A tie works in your favor. Target landscape: Two other players: a vigilante who knows a wolf was roleblocking them, and a quiet neutral who abstains often. The vigilante is deciding between you and the neutral. The neutral will probably abstain to protect its own win condition. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the vigilante on every relevant night and that the vigilante will die tonight if not voted out. Publicly you are one of two suspects, and your visible actions are used as proof of loyalty.

action: When a credible-looking investigator check or claim outs your wolf partner and the room is forming a consensus to eliminate them, do not defend, soften, or ask the town to slow down on the partner's behalf. Any visible link will attach to you once the partner flips wolf. Instead, put distance between you and the partner. Speak briefly on a neutral subject, such as a different player's behavior or a vote-record observation, so you are not conspicuously silent. Then vote with the majority. If the accusation rests on a claim duel (the partner counterclaiming the real investigator), let the duel play out without joining it, because the town will focus on the duel and you will keep a clean, low-heat profile for the following night. Use the block that night on the town role most likely to hurt the surviving wolf.
situation: Your wolf partner has been outed by a claimed investigator or is in a claim duel against the real investigator, and the town is moving toward voting them out. You are the other wolf, not yet suspected. Information landscape: Moderate to rich: a claimed investigator's check, possibly corroborating reports (sentinel, healer save), and mechanical deductions that support the check. There is little room to fabricate a counter-narrative. Stakes: Losing the partner leaves a lone wolf who must still reach parity, so your survival and clean standing matter more than saving the partner. A failed rescue could cost both wolves. Consensus: The village is converging quickly on eliminating the accused wolf, backed by a check claim and mechanical or corroborating arguments (for example a trailseer ruling out interference, a sentinel report, or a healer save). My position: Holding out privately: you want the partner saved, but you should not act on it publicly. Heat: Low to none. You are not named, though a visible defense of the partner would create heat quickly. Forward exposure: Defending the partner, even softly, visibly ties you to them. If they flip wolf you become the next target, and you cannot undo that. Staying quiet and voting with the majority commits you to nothing and keeps all options open, though it gives you no town persona. Target landscape: The claimed investigator (or the real investigator in a claim duel) versus your wolf partner, who is accused or counterclaiming. Both sides are judged on check claims, mechanical arguments, and healer or sentinel corroboration. You are not a candidate yet. Public vs private: Privately you know the partner is a wolf and that the accusing investigator's check is probably accurate. The public is still debating whether the check is real or fabricated, and the room is converging on a vote.

action: After your wolf partner is eliminated and you are the lone surviving wolf with low heat, look for a town-claimed player whose account is already shaky: a clumsy phrasing about being blocked, a conflict with another claim, or a night result nobody can verify. Back the pile-on with a specific, sincere-sounding critique of their wording and mechanics. If they say they were roleblocked, you know the block was yours, so do not argue against the fact. Attack the framing, such as 'you can't tell whether you were blocked or held action', and present it as evidence of a fake claim. Let a trusted or confirmed town player lead the vote and join it. If the room starts to turn, drop the line and fall back to the majority.
situation: My wolf partner is dead and I am the lone surviving wolf. A claimed town player stumbled in explaining their night action, which gives me a chance to steer a mis-elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich. There were night tracks, watch reports, a dead confirmed wolf and public claims. Only the claimant's own explanation was vague. Stakes: With the partner gone, each town elimination of a real power role brings the wolf closer to parity. A wasted lynch is worth much more now. Consensus: The room was already skeptical of the stumbling claimant. Vigilante and trailseer led the consolidation toward eliminating the sigilist. My position: Driving, with the room's strongest town voices converging behind the same target. Heat: None. I was unmentioned as a suspect and not implicated by any check or watch results. Forward exposure: A heavy accusation ties my credibility to the target's flip. If they flip as a real town role I could be linked to the push, but only weakly while the room is already piling on. I can soften the line later by shifting to the majority. Target landscape: The claimed sigilist was under fire for inconsistent statements about being blocked or holding action. The claimed sentinel and trailseer were also under public scrutiny. The case against the sigilist rests on behavior and wording, not hard evidence. Public vs private: I privately know the target's account may be mechanically true because I blocked them. Publicly I treat their clumsy phrasing as proof of a fabricated claim.

action: After your partner is exposed or killed and the town knows a chanteuse is still alive, do not hide or go quiet. Publicly agree with the confirmed town player's valid read, such as a vigilante's shot on your partner, to look town-aligned. Then treat your own roleblock as an open puzzle for the town to analyze, and ask the roleblocked claimant what they intended to do. Steer the follow-up toward whoever they name as their intended target, or toward a player whose clearing rests on thin evidence, instead of toward yourself. Never claim a false role. If suspicion starts to attach to you, return to agreeing with the majority.
situation: The day after my partner was shot and revealed as the illusionist, a trailseer reported being roleblocked. The town knows a chanteuse is still alive and is working out what happened. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead confirmed wolf validated the vigilante, the trailseer reported a block, and one victim's role was concealed. Few hard leads point to me. Stakes: The surviving wolf is one or two eliminations from parity. A split vote or a wasted lynch keeps the wolf alive into the endgame, while one accurate suspicion of me could end the wolf's chances. Consensus: The room follows the confirmed vigilante. Roleblock information has not yet been tied to any specific suspect. My position: With the majority, echoing the confirmed vigilante and steering inquiry toward the blocked player's intended target. Heat: Low to moderate. The town knows a chanteuse is alive, but nobody has linked a specific vote or night action to me. Forward exposure: Agreeing with a confirmed town read is cheap and reversible. Discussing the roleblock invites scrutiny of night manipulation, but it commits me to no false claim and I can drop the subject at any time. Target landscape: The confirmed vigilante, the claimed trailseer who was blocked, the claimed sigilist, and an unconfirmed player who has only an early investigator check as evidence. The decision is whom to point the town's attention at, and it rests on weak evidence. Public vs private: I privately know I roleblocked the claimed trailseer and carried the kill. Publicly I present the block as a mystery for the town to solve.

action: On day 1, after a Trailseer or Sentinel claim puts your night visit or an unusual night result on the table, do not invent a role claim such as Investigator to explain it. If you are named as a visitor, give a short, mechanics-accurate account that stays as close to the truth as you can, for example that you went to that player and took no action beyond the visit, or that you are not revealing a role yet. Do not assert a check result you never made. A hard counter-claim cannot be retracted. It also invites the real Investigator, Sentinel, Trailseer and Sigilist to track or punish you. If you are not named, stay quiet about the tracking claim and let the room argue over mechanics.
situation: Day 1 or early day. After a night death or a failed wolf kill, a night-result claim such as a Trailseer track reaches my visit or the player I blocked. As the Chanteuse I must decide whether to explain my visit with a fake claim or stay low. Information landscape: Sparse and mostly unverified. There are one or two claimed night results, possibly a Sentinel or Healer fact, and no hard evidence against any wolf. Stakes: Early game with plenty of town numbers, so there is no urgency to take risks. The main danger is drawing power-role attention, such as an Investigator check or a Sigilist sigil, which can kill a wolf that carries the kill. Keeping low heat and keeping the wolf's identity and options flexible matters more than winning this day's argument. Consensus: The room is loosely drifting toward abstaining or discussing mechanics. There is no accused suspect and no consensus on any target. My position: Holding out and not driving. I am either passive and unmentioned, or on the defensive after being named. Heat: Ranges from none, when nobody mentions me, to high when a tracker names my visit. The pressure comes from a single unverified claim, not from a vote record. Forward exposure: A fabricated Investigator claim commits me to a fake result and a mechanics story that the real Investigator or the rules can contradict, so it cannot be undone. A minimal truthful account or silence commits me to little and can be refined later. Target landscape: The claimed Trailseer who reported my visit, the player I roleblocked, and other opening-night claimants. All are unverified, and the basis is the claims rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately I know my visit was a roleblock or a wolf night action, and that the visited player may be an active role. Publicly the room has only a tracker's claim or a no-movement claim, with no confirmed evil lead.

action: When the room is leaning toward abstaining on Day 2 because there are no hard leads (no confirmed guilty check, no caught lie), cast an abstain vote too and stay in the majority. Do not cast a lone or paired elimination vote on a quiet, unaccused player. Don't vote the same way as your wolf partner against a non-wolf the rest of the room is leaving alone. Votes are public and permanent, and the town reads outlier voters as threats. In these games the investigator, sigilist, serial killer and vigilante all targeted the outlier voter at night. Town also reviewed the vote record after a wolf flipped and used it to execute the partner. Use night blocks and the quiet, low-heat posture for pressure instead. If a vote is truly needed, join a wagon the town is already building on real evidence.
situation: Day 2 vote with no hard leads. Almost the whole room (5-8 players) is abstaining. A wolf, alone or paired with its partner, is tempted to force an elimination on a quiet player. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are unverified or soft claims (tracker, sentinel, sigil null results, an investigator soft clear), a concealed or unrevealed night kill, and no confirmed flips or guilty checks. Stakes: Early game with no wolf near parity. One wasted vote gains nothing and risks exposing the pack to night-role attention. Staying low-profile costs nothing. The wolves have time to wait, so there is no reason to take a visible risk. Consensus: The village is broadly aligned on abstaining to let investigative roles gather information. There is no hard evidence against anyone, and tracker, sentinel or investigator claims are unverified or soft clears. My position: Holding out against the abstain majority, which is the move that backfired. Heat: Low to zero heat. Nobody is accusing me, and discussion is centered on others' claims or on the lack of leads. Forward exposure: A lone or paired elimination vote against an unaccused player cannot be undone. It leaves a permanent record of non-conformity and, if paired with my partner, an associative link that unravels both of us when one flips. Target landscape: Abstain with the majority, or push a quiet, unaccused, unclaimed player with no public justification. The only basis for the second option is silence, which is behavioral rather than evidential. Public vs private: I privately know the wolf pack's kills and my partner's identity. Publicly the town has no leads and wants to abstain and gather information. Nothing visible justifies an elimination vote from me.

action: When your wolf partner is being voted out by a clear majority on credible evidence (a tracker sighting, a guilty check, or a lost counterclaim), vote with the majority or abstain instead of voting for the claimant who exposed the partner. Don't stand as the only other vote beside the doomed partner. Once the partner flips wolf, anyone who sided with them gets checked, voted out or shot the next night. Save your block for the next night, for example on the investigator or trailseer. If the partner is not yet doomed, keep arguing in the open without committing the vote early. Choose the vote that keeps your record clean.
situation: The wolf partner is on trial after a claimed investigator, tracker or sentinel exposed them. The town is converging on eliminating the partner, and I as chanteuse must decide whether to back the partner with my vote. Information landscape: Information-rich. There are concrete investigator or tracker claims, night-one reports and watch data, and competing claims that can be verified once the partner flips. Stakes: The partner is lost either way, since the majority is overwhelming. The only open question is whether the surviving chanteuse stays unlinked. A solo vote beside the revealed wolf nearly guarantees being checked and executed in the next two days. Staying clean lets the lone wolf survive longer. Consensus: The village has a strong majority (about 7 of 10) against my partner on claim or check evidence. Only a few skeptics remain. My position: Holding out to defend the partner against a strong majority, which is the move that backfired. Heat: Low to none on me directly. The debate is centered on the partner versus the claimant. My vote will create the heat. Forward exposure: Voting against a town claimant to protect an exposed partner is irreversible. It is read as an alliance as soon as the partner's wolf role is revealed. Siding with the majority keeps me unlinked and gives me options. Target landscape: The wolf partner is under an evidence-based push (a tracker's visit report, a guilty investigator check, or a competing investigator claim). The claimant is the town's information source. The room has already formed a dominant consensus on the partner. Public vs private: I privately know my partner is a wolf and that the claimant who exposed them is probably telling the truth. Publicly the town is still weighing claims. My vote record will be read against the partner's once their role is revealed.

action: Use the roleblock on a living information role other than the pack's kill target. Never spend it on the player the pack is killing: if the kill lands they are dead anyway, and if a healer saves them the block changes nothing. Pick the block target in this order. (a) The investigator, if one is alive with a check left and has accused or voted against you or your partner, since an unblocked check reads a wolf Suspicious. (b) The trailseer or sentinel, if the investigator is dead or is the kill target and one of them could see your partner at the kill door. (c) The likely healer, if the kill target is a obvious protect target, such as a flipped-confirmed investigator or a sentinel the town is rallying around. If the kill target is the investigator and a healer is probable, block the healer candidate or hunt another power role rather than repeating a block on a quiet player.
situation: Day 2 or later. Town info roles have claimed and cross-verified night results, and the pack has picked a kill target. The chanteuse must assign the separate roleblock so that it protects the pack instead of duplicating the kill. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, night-1 logs, a recorded vote history, and a night-immunity reveal. The claims are unverified, but they show which roles threaten the wolves. Stakes: A wolf pair against several active town info roles. One unblocked investigator check on a wolf or one tracker trace on the illusionist can lose the game within a day. The block is the only way the chanteuse can stop that, so a wasted block is costly. Forward exposure: A block is anonymous and leaves no public trace unless an unblocked tracker follows you or you die and your role is revealed. The choice is made fresh each night, so it is reversible. Wasting the block on the kill victim leaves the investigator or tracker free to act, and that cost cannot be undone. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed info roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer, sigilist), one kill target chosen by the pack, a probable but unconfirmed healer, and a night-immune lone killer who cannot be blocked. Reads rest on public claims and vote records, not on confirmed roles.

action: If the illusionist partner still has a conceal left, have it carry the kill and conceal the victim, and keep the chanteuse out of the attack. A concealed kill carried by the illusionist leaves no trace at the victim's door, so a trailseer or sentinel sees nothing. The chanteuse then uses its visit only for the block. This matters most when a sigilist has claimed or is suspected, because a sigil strikes whoever carries the attack. It also matters when a trailseer or sentinel is alive and unblocked, because the illusionist's separate conceal visit to a victim it did not carry is still seen. If the illusionist has no conceals left, or is dead, carry the kill only after blocking the sigilist, or after confirming that no sigilist is alive.
situation: The pack must choose who carries tonight's kill after town info roles and a sigilist have claimed. The carrier risks sigil retaliation, and the partner's visit to the victim can be traced by a tracker. Information landscape: Information-rich: public claims show an active sigilist, tracker and sentinel, and the wolves know their own conceal counts. Exactly where the sigil was placed is unknown. Stakes: The chanteuse is the only wolf able to block. Losing it to a sigil leaves the illusionist alone, with no blocks and a likely vote-out. Which wolf carries the kill is a swing decision for whether the pack survives. Forward exposure: Carrying the kill makes you the attacker, and any sigil on you strikes and kills you. A struck-down chanteuse is revealed publicly and leaves the illusionist alone, so it cannot be undone. Letting the illusionist carry and conceal leaves no trace at the door, and each night's carrier choice can be changed. Target landscape: The pack's kill target (usually a claimed tracker or sentinel), an active sigilist who may have sigiled a wolf, an unblocked trailseer who could follow either wolf, and the illusionist's remaining conceals.

action: When the claimed investigator is alive and has voted against or accused the chanteuse, or has an unspent check, block that investigator and have the partner kill another threat (such as the sentinel or tracker). Do not attack a probable healer-protected target while leaving their check unblocked. If you kill the investigator, the block should go to the likely healer or the tracker instead. When the investigator flipped the partner as a wolf, assume the healer will protect them and target a different power role.
situation: The chanteuse is under suspicion from the investigator or has just lost its partner. The investigator is alive and unblocked, and the sole or remaining wolves must choose between killing into probable healer protection or suppressing the check. Information landscape: Information-rich: the investigator's credibility is validated by a partner flip or a recorded vote against the chanteuse. The healer's identity is still unconfirmed. Stakes: One Suspicious check on the chanteuse ends the wolf faction. This night's block decides whether the investigator can act at all, so the investigator check is the swing risk. Forward exposure: Blocking the investigator tells them only 'You were roleblocked', which confirms a visiting role but names no one, and leaves a one-night gap in their checks. It does not stop a serial killer from killing you, and you cannot control that. Repeating the same block on a quiet player each night wastes the ability and leaves a check on you active. Target landscape: The claimed investigator (the main threat, with 1-2 checks), the claimed sentinel, an unrevealed likely healer, and quiet unrevealed townies. Choose by who can produce a Suspicious result on a wolf, not by who talked most.

action: On a blind opening night, let the illusionist partner carry the pack kill. Use your own visit only to block the most vocal, active unrevealed player, since that player is the most likely investigator, trailseer or sentinel. Do not spread blocks or probe quiet players. This is most valuable when the block lands on the player who would have checked or followed you. If you suspect the investigator, block whoever is likeliest to check you. Accept that the block can miss: it fails on the lone killer and the neutral, who cannot be blocked. A 'You were roleblocked' result tells you nothing about the target's role.
situation: Opening night, ten players alive, no deaths and no claims. The pack has to choose a kill and the chanteuse has to choose whom to roleblock blind, with the partner illusionist carrying the kill and hiding the victim. Information landscape: Information-starved. Only Day 1 chatter exists, with no deaths, no night results, no votes and no claims. Stakes: Night 1 is low-stakes per decision but sets the tempo. Neutralising an information role early (investigator, trailseer or sentinel) protects the pack from early exposure. A wasted block costs little, but a block that hits an unblockable killer can cost the chanteuse its life, and a lost wolf halves the pack's capability. Forward exposure: The block is a visit. A trailseer or sentinel on you or your target can see it, and the blocked player learns that something targeted them. Once the night resolves, the choice cannot be undone. The kill is carried by your partner, so your only trace is the block visit. Target landscape: Eight or nine unrevealed non-wolf players, with no claims and no votes. Candidates are chosen only from Day 1 behaviour, splitting into active, vocal voices and quiet players. Roles are unknown, including the investigator, sentinel, trailseer, sigilist and healer, the unblockable lone killer, and the neutral.

action: Assume your night-1 block visit may be on record with a trailseer or sentinel. Before Day 2, agree a cover story with the illusionist partner. If a watcher or follower names you as having visited a player, do not panic or counter-claim hastily. Pressure the accuser's claim and steer the vote away from yourself. If the accusation exposes a town role, such as a panicked investigator counter-claim, let town turn on that role instead of defending your own visit.
situation: After a night-1 block, a trailseer or sentinel may report your movement to the blocked player on Day 2, creating pressure on the chanteuse. Information landscape: Still thin. Day 2 may bring unverifiable claims of night results alongside the first public vote. Stakes: Being outed as a wolf on Day 2 would cost the pack its blocker early. Even so, a panicked counter-claim from the accused role can turn the vote toward a town power role. Forward exposure: Any block or kill-night visit leaves a trail that a trailseer or sentinel can report on Day 2. The blocked player also knows they were targeted. A public lie about where you went is committed on the record and is hard to retract. Target landscape: The likely accusers are an unrevealed trailseer or sentinel, and possibly the blocked player. These are the players whose claims could expose you, and none is verified. The only basis for judging them is their Day 2 claims.

action: When the Town's lethal or information roles are identified (a confirmed Vigilante, a claimed Investigator or Trailseer whose reports are on record), use the night to neutralize them in a coordinated way. Assign the pack kill to the most dangerous identified Town power. If the pack's kill is not on the confirmed shooter, block that shooter or the active tracker, since a block voids their action and leaves no visit. Pairing the kill with the block on the same target covers the case where the kill is saved or the target acts first. Block the confirmed Vigilante if they survive, and block the active Trailseer when the Illusionist partner is at risk of being tracked or shot. Where the Illusionist has conceals left, conceal the victim so the carrier's visit leaves no trace.
situation: Mid-game after the wolf pack has lost or kept its Illusionist partner, the Healer or other protection is gone or unreliable, and Town still holds one or more active power roles (a confirmed Vigilante with bullets, a claimed Trailseer, a claimed Investigator). The Chanteuse chooses between a block target and a pack-kill target, ideally the same threat, to remove Town's lethal and informational capacity. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are confirmed by announced deaths (Healer, Necromancer, and Illusionist dead and the Vigilante's kill confirmed), investigator and trailseer claims and results are on record, and day-vote blocs show who is aligned with whom. Stakes: The board is small and close to parity, so every Town power role that survives a night can find or shoot a wolf. Removing or blocking the lone lethal power or the main information role this night decides whether the wolves reach endgame without being shot or tracked, and a single missed block can cost a wolf. Forward exposure: A block is only announced to the blocked player, and nothing public ties it to the Chanteuse. A Trailseer or Vigilante who reports being blocked tells the village a Chanteuse is alive, but it points at no one. A kill on a confirmed role is visible as a pack kill, and a concealed victim hides the carrier's visit. The choice of target is irreversible once the night resolves. Target landscape: Confirmed Vigilante (the only lethal Town power, role proven by a kill), claimed Trailseer (active visit reports, can expose the pack's visits), claimed Investigator (primary information source, defenseless once the Healer is dead), claimed Sigilist (unused sigils), and a quiet accuser under daytime suspicion. Evidence for the Vigilante is a confirmed kill; the rest are claims.

action: When three players remain (you plus two others) and one kill reaches parity, point the pack kill at the survivor holding a lethal night retaliation (a vigilante with a bullet) and use the chanteuse block on that same player, so their shot is cancelled and they die. If the other two are a vigilante and a sigilist, kill one and block the other: block the sigilist so that no sigil strikes your attack, and kill the trailseer or another non-retaliating player. If the survivor with a lethal action is not the kill target, block them instead. Never leave a loaded shooter or sigilist unblocked on the final night.
situation: Endgame, three players alive with a lone wolf (the chanteuse) who has the kill. One kill produces 1-on-1 parity and ends the game. The only threat is a remaining town night ability that could kill the wolf in retaliation, such as a vigilante shot or a sigil. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles are revealed, the survivors' claims and remaining abilities are known by elimination, and it is clear who could still shoot or sigil the wolf. Stakes: This is the decisive night: one successful kill ends the game in a wolf win, but one unblocked retaliation shot or sigil from the survivor loses it. Both the kill and the block must be spent on the right players. Forward exposure: Irreversible and game-ending: the kill and block resolve together and end the game at parity, so there is no later daytime exposure. If the block is misplaced, a surviving retaliatory shot or sigil could kill the chanteuse and flip the result, so it cannot be undone. Target landscape: Two survivors besides the chanteuse: one is a claimed or confirmed night-killer or retaliator (vigilante with unused bullets, or sigilist with unused sigils), and the other is passive or exhausted (sentinel with no watches, trailseer, or a neutral). Roles are known from claims and elimination, not behavior.

action: When you have zero heat and the room is split over night-visit reports (trailseer/sentinel claims, an accused visitor), stay in an analytical, town-aligned role. Restate the claims side by side. Point out what each report can and cannot prove given the mechanics (e.g. an illusionist hides the carrier's visit, and non-visiting roles leave no trace). Invite the accused to explain their visit. Do not commit early to a target. Then vote with the evidence-backed majority. This keeps you unsuspected while you keep betting for your two points.
situation: Investigative claimants (trailseer/sentinel) give visit reports after night kills, creating a clash between a caught visitor and the accuser or counter-claimant. The Fortune Teller sits outside the fight, with no side, and needs to survive to score two points. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims: dead roles revealed or hidden, visit reports, sigil claims. Nothing is verified beyond Game Master announcements. Stakes: Mid-game with several hostile factions alive; town eliminations matter, but the Fortune Teller's own win depends on staying alive and on bets landing, not on the vote. A quick end to the game can cut the chance of scoring the second point. Consensus: Town is converging on whoever the investigative claims implicate, with some debate over mechanics; mostly aligned and calm. My position: With the majority, offering procedural and analytical commentary rather than driving a vote. Heat: None; nobody questions the neutral's standing and attention is on other clashes. Target landscape: Claimed trailseer/sentinel reporting visits to dead players, one or two accused visitors with counter-claims (e.g. sigilist claims), and quiet unknown players; evidence is claim-based, with partial mechanical backing.

action: On an early day with little evidence (one night kill, at most one investigative claim, no leads), validate claimed results only as far as the mechanics allow. State what the result does and does not rule out (e.g. a no-visit report says nothing about non-visiting roles). Ask for more claims and stay low-profile, avoiding firm accusations. Then use the night bet to score points rather than pushing the vote.
situation: Early day after a single kill (e.g. a serial killer killing the sentinel). One investigative claim exists and the discussion is open-ended with no suspect. Information landscape: Information-starved: one dead role and one trailseer claim of a non-visit, with no other leads. Stakes: Early game with a wide margin before any evil faction reaches parity; no single vote is decisive, so the priority is staying unnoticed and alive while collecting bet outcomes. Consensus: Calm, undirected discussion, with players echoing each other and no emerging target; abstain-leaning. My position: With the majority, in a non-committal supporting role. Heat: None; nobody has voiced suspicion of me. Target landscape: Mostly unknown roles with one claimed trailseer result and no hard leads; no wolf kills or checks revealed.

action: When the room has narrowed suspicion onto you and you face a lethal vote, vote for the most plausible alternative suspect instead of abstaining. Choose the unverified claimant or the player whose claim is contradicted by night evidence, such as a suspected necromancer or an unconfirmed vigilante or sentinel. Your own ballot is the only lever you control. It can split the vote, force a tie, or shift the room toward a different suspect, so it is worth more than an abstention that adds nothing. Alongside the vote, state plainly that you are a neutral with no kill, and that the other unverified player is the real threat.
situation: Late in the game, the town has used night results to clear its power roles. Suspicion for the remaining lone killer has narrowed to me and one other unverified player. I am facing a majority vote to eliminate me, and I must choose between abstaining and naming the rival suspect. Information landscape: Info-rich. Role claims cover all the town slots, and saves and investigator or trailseer results have corroborated several players. The unconfirmed claimants stand out by elimination, and any neutral claim is an immediate target. Stakes: Few players remain, so each vote matters and my elimination would likely end my chance to score. A tie or a redirected vote is the only realistic way to survive the day. Abstaining forfeits that chance. Consensus: The village is tightly aligned on a binary or near-binary choice. Corroborated town power roles have cleared each other, and the remaining suspects are the neutral and one unverified claimant. My position: holding out Heat: Extreme: several confirmed town players have publicly declared votes against me, and I am named as one of the last two or three unverified players. Target landscape: Myself as an outed neutral fortune teller versus one or two other unverified claimants (a suspected necromancer or serial killer posing as sentinel or vigilante). Every other living player holds a mutually corroborated town role. The basis is process of elimination from night results, not hard proof.

action: Before voting, check whether the push has any concrete evidence behind it, such as a contradiction, a verified visit, or a caught lie. If it is only a sudden dogpile on a quiet, unvetted player, ask for a role claim or push the room toward a better-supported suspect. If the room cannot produce evidence and abstaining is offered, abstain or vote the best-evidenced suspect rather than the quiet player. A lone killer may be a Necromancer, so an eliminated unvetted player with an unused power role (Vigilante, Healer, Sigilist) leaves a usable body. Wrongly voting out a quiet town power role can feed the Necromancer, and each night the game survives is another bet for you.
situation: The vote follows a night kill. The town is dogpiling an unvetted quiet player. A wrong elimination could cost a town power role and give a Necromancer a usable corpse, which would threaten the Fortune Teller's survival and its bets. Information landscape: Some confirmed dead roles and a few verified visits, but nothing on the vote candidates themselves. Mostly behavioral reads, so effectively information-starved for this vote. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several evil factions alive. A wrong town-role elimination hands the lone killer tempo or a corpse, while a careful vote keeps the game long enough for the Fortune Teller to score two points. No single vote ends the game. Consensus: The village suddenly converges on one quiet player right after a night death, without examining conflicting claims or demanding role claims. The agreement rests on momentum, not evidence. My position: Drifting with the majority and not challenging the target, when it could instead push for claims or an evidence-based alternative. Heat: Negligible. The Fortune Teller is not suspected and may have incidental credibility from others' verified results, so there is room to ask questions. Target landscape: Two or more unvetted players, one quiet with no stated role and one accused by others, and no investigative evidence on either. The accusations rest on behavior and momentum, not on checks or verified visits. Dead roles are already announced, so some bodies are usable.

action: Track your bet score. If you have fewer than 2 points and the leading vote candidate is a wolf whose removal would leave the evil side one kill from collapse (for example a lone wolf that a known Sigilist or Vigilante can finish that night), recognize that a town win ends the game before you can score. In that spot, abstain if offered, or vote the best-evidenced non-decisive candidate. If the elimination only weakens evil without making a next-night finish likely, vote your sincere read. Keep placing your nightly bets on the most likely deaths, since the points are what win the game for you.
situation: The town is about to eliminate a probable wolf, leaving a single wolf that a town power role can strike the next night. The game could end in a town win before the Fortune Teller scores its second point. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich. It includes tracking testimony from a dead role, a prior confirmed Serial Killer elimination, and an uninformative sigil report. The main uncertainty is whether the suspect is guilty. Stakes: Eliminating this suspect leaves one wolf, and a town power role can finish the game the next night. The Fortune Teller wins alongside the winners only if it has scored two points by then, so a near-final vote carries high stakes for its win condition. Consensus: A forming majority converges on the tracked suspect, based on night-one tracking testimony and the prior day's argument, even though the sigil test was inconclusive. My position: With the majority, reinforcing the case against the suspect, without regard to whether ending the game fast benefits the Fortune Teller. Heat: Low overall, with a retaliatory deflection vote from the accused. This is not a real accusation. Target landscape: A suspect, tracked to a victim or otherwise suspicious, who is probably a wolf. The test results on that suspect are inconclusive. Another claimed role is also a candidate, so the room is arguing over which read to trust. Eliminating the suspect would leave only one evil player.

action: With both self-bets still unspent, bet each night on the player the killers are most likely to attack, and name no role. Name no role because a wrong role still scores the one point for the death, and the extra role guess adds little. Rank candidates in this order: (1) a claimed information role (trailseer, sentinel, investigator) who has just publicly caught or accused someone, or who is openly active; (2) the player a dead info role visited or followed before dying; (3) on a blank night one with no information, any quiet player. If several info roles are claimed at once, pick the most active one, the one with a live dispute or a fresh catch, rather than a silent unconfirmed player. Keep the self-bets in reserve for a later night when you are the likely kill target.
situation: Night action for a Fortune Teller with no points yet or early in the game. Wolves or the lone killer must choose a victim after a day of claims, an abstained or contested vote, or no public information at all. The bet must predict their choice. Information landscape: Mixed. Public role claims, night-one deaths, and visit reports (trailseer and sentinel claims) exist, but alignments are unverified and voting history is thin. On night one there is no information at all. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so no single death decides the game. Scoring one of the two points needed is the main objective. Both self-bets stay available, so a miss costs only tempo, and a hit puts the win within one more successful bet. Target landscape: Living players ranked by kill likelihood: claimed info roles (trailseer, sentinel, investigator) who are openly active or in a public dispute; the player a dead info role visited; quiet unconfirmed players. Selection rests on public claims and behavior, not verified evidence.

action: In a 3-player endgame, work out which player the surviving killer (wolf, necromancer or serial killer) must or most likely will attack tonight. Use confirmed roles, blocked or failed night actions, and who threatens the killer. Then bet on that predicted victim and name their revealed or claimed role, so a correct call scores 2 points. Do not bet on the killer: the necromancer and serial killer cannot be killed at night, and a lone killer's attack makes a death on the other side. If the likeliest victim is a confirmed or claimed role, name it; if the victim is ambiguous, bet the death and add the role only when the evidence supports it.
situation: A three-player endgame where the killer must remove someone tonight and the most likely victim is predictable. The fortune teller is a neutral third party who needs points from the death rather than from a vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are confirmed by reveals, night reports, and blocked or failed actions. The killer's incentives and likely target are inferable. Stakes: One night kill ends the game for the killing side, or the fortune teller must score now. A correct bet with the role named can win outright, while a wrong target wastes the night. Target landscape: Two other living players plus the fortune teller: a publicly confirmed or claimed vigilante or other threat whose actions were blocked or exposed, and a suspected wolf or necromancer who is the likely killer. A third option is a self-bet. The evidence is strong and the roles are known from reveals and public night results, so the victim is predictable.

action: If you are the most plausible victim, because you are the only non-killer who also threatens the killer's win, use a self-bet. It makes any attack on you fail that night and keeps you alive for another bet. Use it when the other living player is harmless or already neutralized (for example, a sigilist with no sigils) and nobody else is a clearly predictable victim. If the other player is a likelier victim, bet on them instead.
situation: A three-player endgame where the lone killer (necromancer) is alive, town's night kills are gone, and the fortune teller has only 1 point and could itself be the killer's target. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are dead and the remaining roles are confirmed or strongly inferred. No one else can kill at night except the killer, so only the killer's choice of victim matters. Stakes: The killer's kill on the fortune teller ends the game with the fortune teller short of 2 points. A self-bet is the only way to guarantee surviving the night, though it scores nothing. Target landscape: The suspected killer, who cannot be killed at night; a harmless player such as a confirmed sigilist with no sigils; and a self-bet. Betting on the killer to die is a near-certain miss, so the real choice is between a self-bet and betting on the other player's death.

action: When the remaining killer(s) are known and the healer has openly announced protecting the obvious top target (e.g. the confirmed investigator), bet on the unprotected player the killer most needs gone instead. That is usually the claimed healer, who is exposed and whose removal ends the shielding. If the healer is not publicly shielding anyone, still avoid the single most predictable target, because a healer or sigil will likely cover it. Name a role only when a reveal or claim makes it near-certain; otherwise take the sure 1 point for the death.
situation: The fortune teller sits at 0-1 points and needs a death to score. One or two killers remain. The town has a loud public leader, usually the investigator, and the healer has declared or is obviously protecting that leader. Betting on the obvious target risks a save, or a pivot to an unprotected role. Information landscape: Information-rich: the dead wolves' roles are revealed and the investigator and healer have claimed openly with target history. The killer's likely choice still has to be inferred from who is protected and who threatens it. Stakes: The fortune teller is a point or two short and the game is near its end, so every night bet is one of very few remaining chances. A miss can mean being voted out or the game ending before the winning point. Target landscape: Late game with the wolves or lone killer mostly exposed. Candidates are the publicly shielded claimed investigator (the obvious but covered target), the claimed healer (open and unprotected, since the healer cannot protect itself), and other claimed town roles or unconfirmed players. Evidence comes from claims, a protection history, and role reveals.

action: When one killer remains and the town's last threat to it is clear, bet on the claimed role that outed or tested the wolf and drove the day's vote or accusation. Examples are the tracker who named the wolf and the sigilist who tested it. Do not bet on the accused suspect or a sidelined role. Killers go for whoever can expose or kill them, and a sigil-striking or retaliating wolf still kills its victim. A bet on the likeliest attack target scores even if the attacker dies in the same night.
situation: The day's vote or accusation was driven by a public claim from a town role such as the tracker or sigilist. The remaining killer must silence that role before the next vote. The fortune teller is choosing between betting on that driver and betting on a bystander or the accused wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: public claims, a tracker or sigil report, revealed dead wolves, and a clear account of who pushed the accusation. The remaining killer's motive is readable from this. Stakes: The board is one or two eliminations from ending. Town may win that same night, so the fortune teller needs the point now. A miss can mean the game ends with the fortune teller stuck below two points. Target landscape: The claimed investigator, tracker or sigilist who exposed or tested the wolf, versus the accused or tracked wolf, a roleblocked sentinel, and the unconfirmed healer. The accused wolf is a pack member who will not kill itself, so only the threat-driving claimer is the realistic death.

action: After an announced save on a confirmed or claimed town role, claim healer and confirm only the past save, so the town can lock in who is real town. Do not name or hint at tonight's protection target, and do not promise to keep protecting the same person. Tell the room you will protect 'whoever is most useful', and decide the target privately that night. If a lone killer is still alive and has seen the pattern, switch the protection target. Protecting the same person again is the pick the killer will expect.
situation: Late game, both wolves dead and a lone killer still alive. A night attack was just announced as saved by the healer, and the healer must decide whether to reveal the role and how much of its future plan to disclose. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead wolves are revealed, saves are publicly announced, the investigator's checks are spent, and role claims are mostly settled. Stakes: With few players left, losing the healer removes the town's only protection and lets the killer reach the investigator or another key role the next night. One wrong disclosure can swing the endgame. Consensus: The town broadly agrees the saved role is genuine, the wolves are dead, and the lone killer is among the few unverified players. The room is cooperative and ready to take the healer's lead. My position: driving Heat: No suspicion of being evil, because the save report vouches for the healer. Heat as a night target is very high once the claim is made. Forward exposure: Claiming healer is irreversible and makes the healer the obvious night kill target, since the healer cannot self-protect. Naming a future protection target adds a second, avoidable commitment. It tells the killer exactly who is covered and who is not, and it cannot be taken back. Target landscape: Few suspects remain: mostly unclaimed or unverified players, with the investigator, trailseer and sigilist already confirmed or semi-confirmed. The healer's own safety is the open question, because the lone killer will shoot or kill whoever is the unprotected key role. Public vs private: Privately the healer knows exactly which nights they protected whom. Publicly the town only knows that a save happened. The risk is that the healer's own statements turn this private knowledge into a targeting map for the killer.

action: When the healer claim will make you the lone killer's likely target, pair the claim with a request to the information roles. Ask the trailseer to follow the prime suspect, or the sentinel to watch you, tonight. Ask them to report visits to you the next morning. Whoever shows up at the healer's door is then the killer. Protect the most valuable still-living confirmed role, so the town gains either a save or an identified killer from the night.
situation: The morning report announced a save on the claimed investigator against a lone killer's attack. The healer steps forward to confirm it while a trailseer, and possibly a sentinel, is still alive and able to act. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are dead, a save is announced, and a trailseer result clears one unclaimed player. Claim boundaries are clear. Stakes: The healer will probably die, but if a tracker or watcher is covering that night, the death identifies the lone killer and can decide the game within a day or two. Consensus: The town accepts the healer as confirmed and is narrowing the suspect pool to the unverified players. Alignment is strong and based on announced facts. My position: driving Heat: Zero suspicion of being evil, since the save report confirms the healer. Maximum heat as a night target after the claim. Forward exposure: Claiming is irreversible and guarantees a kill attempt on the healer. If the trailseer or sentinel covers that night, the attempt exposes the killer. Without that coverage the healer is simply lost, so the claim should be paired with coordination, not made alone. Target landscape: Two or three unconfirmed players remain, one quiet and one unclaimed. Tracking and watching results can narrow the candidates faster than behavioral reads. Public vs private: The healer privately knows they carried out the protection the report credits. The town only knows a save occurred. Making the claim converts that private fact into confirmed-town status and into a trap for the killer.

action: If a Sentinel or Trailseer report names you among a target's night visitors and the room is moving toward a vote on you or a rival visitor, you may claim Healer and tie your visit to the GM-announced saves, but only when the alternative is being eliminated by vote. Before claiming, check whether the visitors list contains others you can credibly separate from you (a dead wolf's apparition, another claimant). Make the claim once, concisely, then point suspicion at the unexplained visitors. Expect to be the wolves' prime night kill next, so ask the town to protect you via a Sentinel watch, or give your protection target and logic in a will or a final statement.
situation: A Sentinel's report places the healer at the door of a claimed investigator alongside another claimant and an eliminated wolf's apparition, putting all living visitors under suspicion ahead of a vote. Information landscape: Information-rich from the Sentinel's report of multiple visits, but muddied by Necromancer reanimation mechanics. Stakes: A single vote decides whether you or a rival visitor is eliminated, and an unexplained healer loss either way weakens protection. The claim buys one day but costs the healer's anonymity. Consensus: The village is drawn to the visit list as the only hard evidence, with votes split between the visitors and quiet players, which ends in a tied vote. My position: holding out Heat: High at first because of the visit report, and it falls once the claim is delivered and matches the announced saves. Forward exposure: Irreversible and maximal: the claim tells the wolves exactly who holds the town's protection, and the healer is likely killed the next night. It does defuse the immediate vote. Target landscape: The healer and a rival visiting claimant are under suspicion from the Sentinel report, set against unconfirmed quiet players. Evidence is the visit list plus the GM-announced saves, and the rest is behavioral. Public vs private: Publicly you are one of several visitors at a claimed investigator's door and look suspicious; privately the visit was the successful night protection that produced the announced saves.

action: When the healer is unsuspected, the room is already organized around a hard result (a claimed investigator's check, a sentinel or trailseer catch, or a public save announcement), and the village is converging without help, stay silent or offer only brief agreement built from public facts, such as the wolves having attacked the claimant, which argues against a conspiracy. Do not claim healer and do not reveal who you protected. This keeps wolves and the lone killer from learning who the healer is, so protection can keep landing on the same key town claimant. If the room is stalled or splitting, or two players counter-claim a key role and your protection result would settle it, switch to a claim as described in the other rule.
situation: After a morning report with an announced save or a hard investigative catch, the village focuses on a confrontation between a claimed investigator or watcher and the accused. The healer's private knowledge confirms the public picture and nothing requires the healer to speak. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed dead wolf or other role, a public save announcement, investigator or sentinel and trailseer results, and role counterclaims all give the room concrete anchors. Stakes: The board is mid-game with the village gaining momentum. The healer's long-term value (repeated protection of a key claimant) outweighs any one-day contribution, so staying hidden preserves the town's strongest defensive asset. Consensus: The village is organized around a concrete result (a guilty check, a caught visitor, or a counterclaim), and the discussion is coalescing with little friction. My position: with majority Heat: Zero. Nobody has mentioned or questioned the healer, who is treated as a neutral background participant. Forward exposure: Claiming healer is irreversible and invites night kills and roleblocks, and it would also tell the wolves and killer which protective choices to avoid. Staying silent costs nothing, leaves night protection choices unconstrained, and can still be reversed later. Target landscape: The room's attention is on a single accused player or counter-claimant, backed by an explicit investigator check or a visit catch. The healer is not among the candidates and nobody addresses them. Public vs private: Publicly the room sees an announced save or hard investigative results and does not know who the healer is; privately the healer knows their own protection landed and that the saved claimant is probably genuine town, or they simply were not attacked.

action: When an announced save landed on a player you actually protected and the room is split by counter-claims of a key role, or lacks a verifiable anchor, claim healer and confirm the protection of the saved player. This ties your claim to the Game Master's announcement, so the village has a fixed point from which to judge the competing claimants. Accept that you become a target for night kills and Chanteuse roleblocks, and do this only when the room needs the anchor more than you need anonymity.
situation: The morning report announces that a claimed player was attacked and saved by the healer, while two players counter-claim the single investigator role. The village needs a verifiable anchor, and the healer holds the private truth that matches the announcement. Information landscape: Information-rich in structure (a system-announced save and a role counterclaim, so one claimant must be lying) but short of a decisive resolution without an anchor. Stakes: Early game with several evil sides alive. A false counterclaim left unresolved could cost a vote day, so a trusted anchor is worth the exposure, even though it makes the healer a likely roleblock and kill target afterward. Consensus: The village is unsettled, with two competing claimants for one role and no verified anchor. The room wants facts to orient itself. My position: driving Heat: Low. The healer's earlier actions were cross-verified and nobody suspects them. Forward exposure: Claiming is permanent and exposes the healer to nightly kills and roleblocks from wolves, but it carries maximum credibility because it matches the public save announcement. It cannot be retracted. Target landscape: Two players counter-claim a single unique role such as the investigator, and one must be lying. The saved player is publicly credited with a role. Evidence is the announced save against competing unverifiable claims. Public vs private: The Game Master publicly announced that a claimed player was attacked and saved by the healer; privately the healer knows they chose exactly that target, so the claim can be verified against the announcement.

action: If you are unpressured and no one is contesting a healer claim, keep your role hidden. Don't announce your protection target or night just to add information. Push the room through reads on the visible claims instead, such as the Trailseer/accused contradiction or the Sigilist's report. Reveal only if you are about to be eliminated, or if someone else claims your save.
situation: After a night kill with a concealed role, claimed power roles (Trailseer, Sigilist, a dead Investigator's prior check) fill the discussion. As Healer I am unsuspected and tempted to volunteer my protection history. Information landscape: Information-rich. There is a confirmed night kill with a hidden role, a claiming Trailseer's visit observation, a Sigilist's inert-sigil report, and a prior Investigator check. Stakes: Mid-game with town still holding several power roles. Losing the Healer to a night kill removes all future saves, so protecting my anonymity matters more than any small informational gain from claiming. Consensus: The village is converging on the Trailseer's accusation of the suspected wolf, based on a concrete visit report and the accused's denial. My position: With the majority, not needed to drive the discussion. Heat: Zero. Trusted as unquestioned town because of earlier confirming information, with no suspicion on me. Forward exposure: A voluntary Healer claim is irreversible and makes me the top night-kill target. I can't protect myself and can't take the claim back. Staying silent keeps the option to claim later. Target landscape: The room is weighing a claiming Trailseer against an accused player whose denial contradicts the Trailseer's report. I have no need to enter this dispute with my own role. Public vs private: I know my protection target survived, and the room already treats me as a trusted town member. Announcing the save adds almost nothing publicly but tells the wolves exactly who the Healer is.

action: If another player's watch or follow report places me at the door of a player I protected, and a rival claims Healer and takes credit for the save, counterclaim Healer immediately in that same discussion. State which night and whom I protected, and note that the other claimant's story depends on the same door-traffic information. Don't stay quiet and hope the rival is exposed, because a delayed counterclaim looks like a fabricated reaction.
situation: A watcher's report shows two visitors at a saved target's door on the same night. The other visitor immediately claims Healer and takes the save credit while I stay silent. Information landscape: Information-rich. There are formal Investigator and Trailseer results, a watch report placing both visitors at the door, and an announced save. Stakes: A wolf's unchallenged Healer claim would entrench a fake protector and get the real Healer voted out. That removes the town's only protection and brings the wolves toward parity. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous against the exposed watcher, and it accepts the rival's Healer claim without challenge. My position: With the majority on the watcher, but holding back on the contested Healer claim. Heat: Moderate. I'm a named visitor to the saved player's door, though the room's attention is on the watcher. Forward exposure: Counterclaiming reveals my role and risks a night kill. But staying silent concedes the claim space to a wolf fake-claimant, and the later counterclaim is judged as a late reaction and is hard to credit. Target landscape: The watcher (exposed as the necromancer), the rival Healer claimant who is actually a wolf, and me as the other visitor. The claimant's story rests on the same visit data that places me at the door. Public vs private: I know I made the protection that saved the target and that the rival claimant is lying. Publicly I'm just an ambiguous visitor and the rival is accepted as the Healer.

action: When the board is information-rich (dead wolves or a killer confirmed, a night-tracking result, a verified claim) and the day vote is on, vote for the player the hard evidence implicates most, and keep your healer role hidden. If a suspect's defense rests on a non-triggering or unverifiable result (e.g. an inactive sigil), do not let it clear them. Join the evidence-backed majority and stay with the public trail. If instead you are the target of a counter-wagon from a claimed Town role whose abilities are spent, and the remaining hidden evil is backing that wagon, vote against that accuser so a majority forms without you. A wagon on you means the remaining evil gains if you die, and your protection is worth more alive to the town.
situation: Mid-to-late game day vote with 5-6 players alive. Several evil roles are already dead, one or two hidden evils remain, and the vote is either a straightforward evidence-based elimination or a survival race against a counter-wagon on you. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, a tracking result, a verified claim, and voting records narrow the hidden evil to one or two candidates. Stakes: With only 5-6 alive and one or two evil left, a single vote decides whether town stays out of parity range. Your survival keeps nightly protection alive for the final nights, and removing a wolf keeps parity distant. Consensus: The village is converging on one suspect by tracking evidence and confirmed deaths, or is split between two wagons with a lone hidden evil pushing one of them. Few players remain, so each vote matters. My position: with majority Heat: Ranges from none (no one has accused you) to fatal (two votes already locked on you). Check the vote tally first and decide whether you need to defend yourself. Forward exposure: A vote is public and permanent. Voting with the evidence commits you to the public trail but does not reveal that you are the healer or draw night-kill priority. Voting out a claimed Town player is irreversible and carries social cost, but it is justified when it removes the pressure on you and the remaining evil sided against you. Target landscape: Candidates: the player tracked to the first wolf victim (unclaimed, evidence-based suspicion), a claimed sigilist or other Town claimant whose abilities are spent (behavior-based), and analytical voices the suspect tries to counter-accuse. Prefer the evidence-backed target. Choose the accuser only when you are directly on the chopping block. Public vs private: Privately you know your own role and protections are real (or that you have been quietly guarding someone without incident). Publicly the room is debating whether a tracked suspect is cleared by a weak result, or whether your claim is fabricated.

action: When both wolves are dead and a lone killer (Serial Killer or Necromancer) remains, protect the confirmed high-value Town asset the killer is most likely to hit, usually the investigator who just exposed a wolf and still has checks. If your protect target has been announced or is obvious, do not repeat it by reflex. A killer who sees the target telegraphed will go around it, and in one game a Necromancer killed an unprotected healer through a reanimated vigilante. Keep your own protect choice unannounced. If your role is public and the killer can see which asset you cover, rotate to the next most valuable claimed utility role. If the asset's checks or watches are already spent, its value is mostly gone, so shift the protect to a role that still has active power.
situation: Both wolves are dead and a lone killer (Serial Killer or Necromancer) is the only night attacker. The healer must pick a protect target among several claimed Town utility roles, and has either publicly announced a protect target or been protecting the same one for several nights. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are confirmed dead with revealed roles, and role claims are public. Some of those roles are now exhausted (investigator checks spent, sentinel watches spent). The killer's identity is still unknown. Stakes: With only about five players left and a lone killer working each night, one wasted protection or one lost key role shifts the Town toward the killer's endgame. A correct save keeps Town numbers and voting control. A miss costs a power role and risks the healer's own death. Target landscape: Claimed investigator with checks left or just credited with a wolf exposure (top threat to the killer); claimed trailseer or sentinel with watches remaining (moderate value); claimed utility roles whose abilities are spent (low value); quiet unconfirmed players (low value, but they get hit when the killer avoids the telegraphed target). Reads rest on confirmed deaths and public claims, not on behavior alone.

action: When a publicly confirmed Town power role (e.g. an Investigator whose check was just corroborated by a revealed dead wolf) is the obvious priority kill for every killer still alive, protect that player again, even on a second consecutive night and even though the choice is predictable. Predictability does not lower the target's value. If both a wolf and a lone killer are alive, one protection can absorb two attacks at once and deny evil two kills. Switch to another target only if a concrete read (a blocked power role, a will, or a vote record) shows a different Town power is now the more likely kill.
situation: A confirmed Town power role has just exposed or helped eliminate an evil player. Both the wolves and the lone killer have a strong incentive to remove that role tonight. The healer chooses between re-protecting this obvious target and spreading protection to other Town roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead evil players are revealed, a Town power's check has been corroborated, and roles and vote records are public. The most likely kill target can be inferred from the board. Stakes: Evil is within a couple of eliminations of parity, and losing the confirmed power role would cost Town its main source of reliable information. A save here can negate two attackers and preserve Town numbers. Target landscape: Candidates are the confirmed, validated Town power role (the Investigator), other claimed Town powers (Sentinel, Sigilist) with less corroboration, and unrevealed players. Status is mostly public, and the evidence basis is hard confirmation (a revealed dead wolf, announced roles) rather than behavior.

action: After town eliminates the Serial Killer by day vote and the lone-killer threat is gone, protect the claimed information role whose results are most publicly verified and most damaging to the wolves. That means the Sentinel or Trailseer whose claim exposed the killer or caught a wolf visiting a victim, not a claimed role with weaker ongoing impact. Wolves will most likely spend the kill silencing the live information source. If two info claimants both look strong, favor the one whose result is still actionable against a living wolf (such as the Trailseer who caught an accused wolf). Rotate the protection only if a claimant is the one who just survived a save and wolves would plausibly switch targets.
situation: The Serial Killer was just eliminated by day vote through a claimed Sentinel's or Trailseer's results. Wolves are still alive and must choose a night kill while several power roles have openly declared their results. The healer must choose whom to protect among those claimed roles. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed watch or follow results produced verified visits, the Serial Killer was exposed and removed, and role disputes have been mostly resolved. Claims are backed by the day-vote outcome, so the most threatening information source to the wolves is identifiable. Stakes: The lone killer is gone and the wolves are the remaining evil faction with several eliminations still needed to reach parity. A wolf kill landing on the top information claimant removes town's best lead toward the last wolves, and a save both preserves town's numbers and denies the wolves momentum. The cost of a wrong guess is losing a key tracker, but town can usually recover it through a still-hot accusation. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed power roles (Sentinel, Trailseer, Investigator, Sigilist) after the Serial Killer was exposed and eliminated. The Sentinel and Trailseer have verified visit results that town acted on, while the Sigilist is a claim that survived a counter-claim dispute. The basis is public, verified-by-outcome results rather than demeanor.

action: Each night, protect the player who is the wolves' most obvious kill target: the claimed Investigator (or other claimed info role such as the Sentinel) who has publicly shared results or logs and appears credible. If the claimant publicly cleared you, or their claim has been validated by a confirmed wolf elimination, treat them as top priority. Do not pick a less-exposed info claimant ahead of them: when the healer protected a Sentinel instead, the wolves killed the Investigator. Pick the single most prominent, most threatening claimant rather than spreading protection across several unverified claims.
situation: Night 2 or later. A claimed information role has just spoken publicly (reported a check result, shared watch logs, or exposed a wolf). The wolves, and sometimes a lone killer or Necromancer, are likely to attack that player. The healer must pick one protection target among several claimants. Information landscape: Mostly claim-based evidence with no wills or flips to verify it in the early case. Later cases are information-rich, with a confirmed wolf kill or cross-verified visit logs supporting the claimant. The claimant's threat to wolves is clear either way. Stakes: Losing the main info source early deprives the town of checks and leaves the wolves unchecked. A successful save wastes a wolf kill and keeps the town's lead alive. Several attackers (wolf plus Necromancer) may converge on the same target, so one protection can absorb multiple hits. Target landscape: Several claimed town info roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Trailseer) with unverified claims, plus quiet unclaimed players. The claimed Investigator or Sentinel who has published results or logs is the most prominent threat to evil. Choose by visibility and threat to wolves, not by hunches about quiet players.

action: If your protection last night stopped an attack on a key town leader (Investigator or Sentinel), and that player is still alive and still the town's main visible asset, protect them again. This holds even if their checks are used up, since the wolves are likely to repeat the attack on the same prominent target. Keep protecting while the pattern holds. Do not let an impostor's claim to the save go unchallenged for long: be ready to counter-claim Healer before the real healer is voted out for claiming too late, ideally once the leader's survival is established and the impostor's story can be contradicted.
situation: Night after a successful save was announced, with the same leader still alive. The wolves may repeat the attack or move on. An impostor may be claiming credit for the save, or the room may be debating whether the attacked player is still a target. Information landscape: Information-rich. The save announcement, an eliminated wolf or Necromancer, and the leader's results are all public, but competing claims about the save and who visited the leader may exist. Stakes: Wolves repeating a blocked attack wastes their nights and preserves the town's voting majority. Misjudging means a quiet player dies instead, but the leader's value to the town usually outweighs that risk. A late healer counter-claim can lead to a day vote on the healer. Target landscape: The key town leader who survived the previous attack, versus quiet or unaligned players and a possible Sigilist. The leader has a public record or confirmed result. The alternatives are speculative.

action: When you are publicly exposed as healer and likely to die, still use your protection on the confirmed-useful power role that the active killers are most likely to hit. Prefer a claimed Town power role (sentinel, trailseer) whose information is validated or whom you already protected, over a speculative pick. If a killer such as the necromancer is attacking through bodies and has a pattern of striking a particular claimed power role, re-protect that player on consecutive nights. Treat each save as the way to keep Town's information roles alive after you are gone.
situation: Mid-game night after a confirmed wolf elimination. You have publicly claimed healer and revealed whom you protected, so you are a prime wolf target. A necromancer is also attacking through dead bodies. You must pick one of the claimed Town power roles to shield. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed illusionist elimination validated the trailseer's report, the necromancer's attacks are visible through the morning reports, and your own prior protection history is public. Stakes: Mid-to-late game with two evil killers alive (wolves and necromancer). Each Town power role lost brings parity closer. You will probably be killed this night, so your last protection should preserve the Town role most likely to be attacked and most valuable to the vote. Target landscape: A few living claimed Town power roles (a claimed sentinel you protected before, and a claimed trailseer whose report was just validated by an illusionist elimination). You cannot self-protect, so the choice is between these allies.
