The weakest point is whichever fact depends on a single unverifiable statement. Public vs private: Privately I carried the night kill through a reanimated body and know I am the lone killer. Publicly I am only the odd one out in a three-way endgame, and I must look like a plain town role.

action: In a 3-4 player endgame where you are cornered and have no majority, put your vote where the room's accusation already points, so you join a majority instead of holding out against it. If a claimed town player demands that the unclaimed players step forward, vote the other unclaimed player rather than the claimed town player. That player is the likeliest wolf or hidden evil. Say plainly that the claimed role has behaved consistently and that the other unclaimed player is the one dodging. This pulls the claimed town player to your side and leaves the other unclaimed player as the lone target. If the claimed town player's role is already contradicted by confirmed deaths or tracking, switch to the other town survivor and offer reasoning that is checkable against public facts. Never counter-vote the sole town claimant who is pressuring you unless another voter will back you. A vote cast alone cannot be taken back and leaves you with one vote against two.
situation: Late endgame (3-4 alive) day vote. A claimed town player forces the unclaimed players to step forward, or the two surviving town players coordinate to eliminate me. I am the necromancer and I am cornered as the odd one out. Any two votes against me end the game. Information landscape: Information-rich: all previous dead roles and abilities were publicly revealed, and claims have been cross-checked against night tracking. There is little room left to bluff. Stakes: With four or fewer alive, one vote decides survival. If I am eliminated, the game goes to town or the wolves immediately. If I survive and one more player dies, I am a step from my own win condition of at most one other player alive. I need to join a plurality, not stand alone. Consensus: The remaining village is tightly aligned and well informed. Dead roles were all revealed, and claims have been cross-referenced against night results, so the unrevealed players are boxed in. My position: holding out Heat: Extremely high: the claimed town players are explicitly pressing the unclaimed players, or have already coordinated against me. The basis is failing to claim a role, or a fake claim contradicted by the tracking results. Forward exposure: The final vote is public, permanent and irreversible. A counter-vote against a town claimant who is not backed by anyone shows I am isolated and hands the opposing pair a ready two-vote majority on me. Joining the existing accusation commits me to nothing beyond that vote and can still be explained afterward. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed town players (Vigilante, Sentinel, Trailseer or Sigilist, whose claims are backed by public flips and tracking) and the other unrevealed player, who is the likely wolf or hidden evil. Evidence for the claimed players is strong and consistent. Evidence against the other unclaimed player is behavioural: no claim, and a silence the town has already noticed. Public vs private: Privately I am the necromancer, still working through dead bodies. Publicly I am an unrevealed or thinly-claimed player under pressure to show a role, and my fake or absent claim is easy to cross-check against the night results town has traded.

action: When your heat is low and the vote is forming around a player whose claim or story is mechanically contradicted by the rules, vote with the majority on that player instead of siding against the investigative claimant. If the eliminated player is revealed as a wolf, note the announced body and plan reanimated attacks, or blocks if it was the Chanteuse, from the next night. If the majority target turns out to be Town, you still keep a clean public record.
situation: A concealed night death produced a claimed visit report that points at an unconfirmed player. That player denies it and disputes the mechanics, and the day vote splits closely over whether the claimant or the accused is lying. Information landscape: Information-rich. Several claims are on the table (Trailseer, Sentinel, Sigilist) and a role was hidden by an illusionist. The rules let players test whether each claim is mechanically possible. Stakes: A single vote can decide a near-tied elimination. Removing a wolf also supplies a usable body for your later night attacks. Mid-game with many players alive, a lasting record of backing the wrong side is costly. Consensus: The room is nearly split, about 5-4. Both sides argue from claimed night results and from interpretations of the visit and concealment rules. My position: Tempted to hold out against the eventual majority. Heat: Low. You are seen as a normal town participant in a mechanical dispute, with no one pointing at you. Forward exposure: Voting against an information claimant commits you publicly to an anti-information stance. It becomes permanently suspicious if that claimant is later proven right, and a vote cannot be undone. Voting with the majority leaves a record that cannot be held against you. Target landscape: The binary split is between a claimed investigative role (Trailseer, Sentinel, Investigator) reporting a visit and an accused player who denies it and attacks the mechanics. The accused is unconfirmed. The claimant's report fits the rules, and the denial rests on a mechanical argument. Public vs private: Privately you want dead wolves to leave announced bodies you can use. Publicly you look like an ordinary town player arguing over how tracking interacts with illusionist concealment.

action: If your reanimated-body result has been exposed as impossible for any living role and the room is converging on you, spend your last word and your vote on spreading suspicion instead of a lone retaliation. Name the players who actually visited the claimant's door, or other claimants whose stories conflict, as the alternative suspects. Cast your vote on one of them so the room has a competing target, and do not vote alone against the accuser. Better still, do not reveal a body-derived result publicly.
situation: Your claimed watch or check result mechanically outs you as using a dead player's body. The trusted claimant leads the village toward voting you out. Information landscape: Information-rich. A dead role was announced, your claimed result is mechanically impossible for any living role, and the claimant has credibility after surviving an attack. Stakes: Your own elimination is near-certain, and it ends the lone-killer path to victory. Only splitting the vote or planting a plausible alternative suspect can change the result. Consensus: Strong consensus to eliminate you, built on hard mechanics: an announced dead role plus a result that only a necromancer could hold. My position: Holding out alone against the room. Heat: Critical. The village recognizes your reported result as mechanically impossible for any living role except the necromancer. Forward exposure: A lone retaliatory vote on the accuser confirms total antagonism and gives you no allies or deflection. Redirecting onto the visitors keeps a competing story alive and can still be dropped if the room rejects it. Target landscape: The claimed investigator is widely trusted after surviving an attack and is the village's spearhead. The two visitors at that player's door are alternative targets with some evidence behind them. Your own claim is the one under mechanical suspicion. Public vs private: You know you used a dead role's body to get the result, and the village correctly sees that only a necromancer could have it. Your real position is exposed, while your public stance still claims an ordinary role.

action: If your only usable body is a revealed dead wolf (Illusionist or Chanteuse) and town has public healer, sentinel and trailseer claims, attack through the Illusionist's body instead of blocking. First check whether the Illusionist still has conceals left, because a kill then hides the victim's role and removes the trace from watchers. Pick a target the healer cannot cover. The healer can never protect itself, so a credible claimed healer is the cleanest kill. If the healer has publicly named a habitual protectee (usually the investigator), do not attack that player, because the save will confirm your target as Town and announce a reanimated wolf for nothing. Otherwise attack a claimed sentinel or trailseer that the healer is unlikely to cover. Remember the attack reads Suspicious to any living investigator that night.
situation: First reanimation night, right after a wolf (Illusionist) was executed and revealed. Several Town power roles have claimed publicly and the healer's protection habits are partly known. The necromancer must choose between attacking, blocking or staying put. Information landscape: Information-rich: the dead wolf's role is system-confirmed, healer saves have been announced, and public claims plus voting records exist. The healer's night choices are still unverified. Stakes: The necromancer is not yet near winning, so every kill counts. A blocked attack wastes the one-use reveal of your activity and thins nothing. A successful kill of a protector or watcher opens the board for the later kills the necromancer needs. Forward exposure: The morning report will say killed by or attacked by a reanimated wolf, which confirms a Necromancer is active. It also makes you read Suspicious to a living investigator that night. A failed attack gives the town information and kills no one. The announcement cannot be undone, but a concealed role denies the town the victim's role information. Target landscape: One usable body (the dead Illusionist). Living candidates are the claimed healer (cannot self-protect), the claimed sentinel, the claimed trailseer, the claimed investigator (likely the healer's repeat protectee), and unclaimed players. Healer and sentinel are claims only, and the protection pattern comes from claims and past saves, not hard evidence.

action: If you are already under suspicion (tied or heavily voted last day, or a sentinel or trailseer is publicly active) and your only body is a dead Chanteuse, stay put that night. Do not roleblock the investigator or healer. A block makes a visible visit that a watching sentinel or trailseer sees, and it strips Town of protection so that the wolf's kill lands. It does nothing to relieve the vote pressure on you. Staying put reads Not suspicious to an investigator and leaves no trace. Use the night to let the wolves and Town fight, and revisit blocking or attacking only once the heat has dropped or you have a target that does not point back to you.
situation: The necromancer has survived a tied or contested vote and is the prime suspect. Town is rallying around a claimed investigator and healer, and a sentinel is reporting visit patterns. The necromancer is tempted to roleblock a central Town role with the dead wolf's body. Information landscape: Information-rich: the voting record, a sentinel's reported visits, healer and investigator claims, and revealed dead roles are all public. Town can cross-check any visible reanimation. Stakes: A single tie or vote could remove you. Extra scrutiny on non-cleared players is what ended these necromancers, so avoiding new evidence matters more than the small gain from a block. Forward exposure: Holding commits you to nothing and is fully reversible. You give up one night of action, but you stay invisible to sentinel and trailseer, read Not suspicious on an investigator check, and make no public announcement. Target landscape: Dead Chanteuse body only. Possible block targets are the claimed investigator (checks already used), the claimed healer, and active accusers. Blocking any of them is visible to a sentinel watch on that target and benefits the wolves more than you.

action: When a freshly eliminated Town attacker's body (e.g. the vigilante) becomes usable, reanimate it and shoot the highest-value information or protection role confirmed on the board. Branch on who is protected. If the healer has publicly claimed and named tonight's protection target, shoot the healer, not the protected player. If no healer is exposed, shoot the confirmed sentinel or trailseer, whose watches could trace your visits. Pick the target whose death also removes the town's ability to catch you.
situation: Midgame, a Town attacker such as the vigilante was just voted out and its role was announced, giving the necromancer a fresh usable body. Several Town investigative and protective roles are still alive alongside a surviving wolf. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are confirmed through announced deaths and public night reports, and the healer has hard-claimed and stated protection targets. The town's investigative picture is well developed. Stakes: With about six alive and the town already thinned by wolf kills, each successful necromancer kill moves the board toward you being one of the last two alive. A failed or blocked kill hands the town a tempo to narrow the field and vote you out. Forward exposure: A reanimated-vigilante kill is announced publicly and reads Suspicious to an investigator that night, so the town learns a necromancer is active. It cannot be undone. The cost is acceptable only when the kill removes a role that threatens you, and the shot has no miss penalty. Target landscape: Confirmed sentinel, claimed investigator, a healer who has openly named the player they protect, and unconfirmed claimants (trailseer, sigilist). Roles are confirmed by public night reports, announced deaths and the healer's own claim. The choice rests on evidence of who threatens or shields the town, not on behavior reads.

action: After a night where the healer visibly saved your target, switch targets and do not retry the same protected player. The healer will probably protect them again, especially if the healer has claimed and named them. Aim the usable body at a different high-value target: the suspected or claimed healer, or an unprotected investigative role among the quiet players. If no healer is identifiable, pick the next most dangerous unprotected role. If you must choose between a protected player and an unprotected one, choose the unprotected one.
situation: The previous night's attack through a body was announced as saved by the healer, so a protection pattern is public. Only a limited set of bodies remains available, and the town is trying to identify you. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: the morning report confirmed the save, and the protected player is publicly known. The healer's identity may or may not be known. Stakes: Each wasted attack night lets Town investigative and protective roles survive and gives them time to narrow the suspect pool toward the necromancer. Breaking the protection pattern is worth more than repeating a known-blocked kill. Forward exposure: A repeat attack on the same target would be announced again as a reanimated strike and read Suspicious to an investigator, and would likely fail, which burns a night and keeps the town alert. Switching targets costs nothing extra in exposure and can be changed again each night. Target landscape: The claimed investigator who was already saved once and is likely protected again, versus the unknown or claimed healer and passive town roles among the quiet players. Evidence for protection comes from the morning save report and the healer's claim.

action: When 3 players are alive (you plus two others), all wolves are dead, and at least one attack-capable body is announced (dead Vigilante, or dead Illusionist), use that body to attack one of the two others and reach 2 alive. This ends the game at once. Prefer the Vigilante body because a sigil cannot punish an attack made through a body. Pick the target the Healer is least likely to be protecting. If a confirmed Healer is alive, strike the other player. If the Sigilist has no sigils left, it cannot hurt you, so it is a safe target. Do not wait a night.
situation: The last wolf was voted out in the day. Three players are alive going into the night, so one kill finishes the Necromancer win condition of two players alive. Information landscape: Info-rich. Dead wolf and Sigilist roles are confirmed, remaining abilities are known, and the Vigilante body is usable because its role was announced. Stakes: One successful kill decides the whole game. A failed attack, such as a Healer save, only delays the finish, but the town gets another day to vote you out. Forward exposure: None. If the strike lands the game ends before the town can react. The only way to lose the tempo is a Healer save, and then you can repeat the attack next night. Target landscape: Two living players besides you, such as a confirmed Sigilist with no sigils left and an unconfirmed player. The dead Vigilante's body is available. No living player can stop the strike except a Healer, and none was confirmed.

action: At 4 alive, when you need two more kills, spend the night attack on the living player who is still actively gathering information and could identify you. This means a Trailseer who is still following players, or a Sentinel or Investigator with checks left. Do not target a role that has already used up its abilities, because the live tracker will still read your visits and lead the vote against you. Use a Vigilante body (no miss penalty) or an Illusionist body (hides the victim's role) for the attack.
situation: Four players are alive after a day vote. The town's remaining tool is a tracker or watcher whose night results can narrow the lone killer down to you. You must pick between an exhausted role and an active one. Information landscape: Mostly info-rich. Most town roles are accounted for, and the active information roles and who has used up their abilities are publicly claimed or inferable. Stakes: You need two more eliminations while the town needs only one correct vote. Removing the one living player who can verify visits decides whether the next day vote lands on you. Forward exposure: An attack night reads Suspicious to an Investigator, and the morning names a reanimated attacker, so the town learns a Necromancer exists. The kill cannot be undone. Wasting it on a harmless target leaves the tracker alive to confirm who did not visit, which exposes you. Target landscape: Living candidates: an Investigator with zero checks left, a claimed Trailseer who is tracking each night, and an unclaimed Sigilist. Choose by remaining capacity to expose you, not by how loudly a player has accused others.

action: At 4 alive, when a confirmed Vigilante still has a bullet and the town is discussing using it on the lone killer, use a dead Chanteuse's body to block the Vigilante. A blocked Vigilante does nothing and makes no visit, and a block is not an attack. Do not attack the Vigilante: the Healer will likely protect that player, and the Vigilante's shot can still land on you. If no Chanteuse body is usable, attack the player most likely to be left unprotected, rather than the village's obvious protection priority.
situation: Four players are alive after both wolves and the Sigilist have died. An armed, publicly confirmed Vigilante is openly considering shooting the lone killer, and the Healer's protection priority on the Vigilante is predictable. Information landscape: Info-rich. The Vigilante is publicly confirmed, both dead wolf bodies have announced roles, and the Healer is expected to protect the Vigilante. Stakes: You need two more eliminations. The Vigilante's single bullet can end the game in a town win if it lands on you, so neutralizing it matters more than forcing a kill into a predicted save. Forward exposure: A block leaves no morning announcement, so it is nearly invisible. Blocking the Vigilante gives up a kill that night. An attack on a predictably protected target wastes the kill and leaves you open to the Vigilante's shot. Target landscape: The confirmed Vigilante with one bullet, a claimed Healer, and a neutral Speculator are alive. A dead Illusionist and a dead Chanteuse are both usable. The Vigilante is the only living player who can kill you at night.

action: On Day 2, once a night death or a peaceful night gives your watch result real value, claim Sentinel and report it exactly: name the watched player and every visitor, or say that no one visited. Do this early, before other claims harden. Branch on the result. If the visitor list contains a player who visited a freshly killed victim and has not been cleared, name that player as the lead and push the vote on them. If the visitors are claimed town roles, ask them to confirm their own movements so the town can cross-verify. If the watch caught nobody, say so, and use it to narrow who the killer could be. Accept that the claim makes you a night-kill and roleblock target. Report the result anyway, because a verifiable mechanical lead on a day with a vote is worth more than staying hidden. Hold your second watch for a night when you can use it, and ask the healer or others to keep you covered.
situation: Day 2 discussion opens after Night 1, with either a death or a no-death morning. The Sentinel holds a private watch result showing who visited a victim or a target, and the town is still comparing claims with no strong leads. Information landscape: Information-starved publicly, with announced deaths and a few unverified role claims. The Sentinel's private visitor list is the highest-value hard evidence on the table. Stakes: Early game with a comfortable margin, so no single vote flips the game. Still, the first vote can remove the lone killer if the lead is sound. Disclosing early gives town its best chance at that, while the exposure risk is manageable if a healer is alive. Consensus: The village is calm and has no hard leads, with only early role claims and a death or a quiet night. It is ready to build on any verifiable report, and no accusation is gaining ground yet. My position: Driving the room by supplying the first concrete information, with the village following along. Heat: Near zero. The claim comes unprompted and is mechanically checkable, so it reads as helpful town information rather than a fishing claim. Forward exposure: Irreversibly reveals the Sentinel role and one spent watch, and makes you a priority target for the wolves' kill and the Chanteuse's block. The claim is hard to retract, but the visitor list can be cross-checked by town roles who also visited, which gives it credibility. Target landscape: The players named as visitors, whether unverified or claimed town, plus the dead victim whose door was watched. The basis is a mechanical visit record, not behavior. Visitors who are claimed town roles can corroborate each other. An unverified visitor to a murder victim is the strongest lead. Public vs private: Privately holds an exact visitor list for a night, usually the victim's or a suspect's door. Publicly the town knows only the death announcements and unverified claims, so the list is information nobody else has.

action: When you hold a watch result that places named visitors at a death or attack scene, open the day discussion by claiming sentinel and reporting the full visitor list verbatim. Include the night and the watched player, and demand each named visitor explain their visit. Then branch on the answers. If a visitor claims a role whose ability needs a visit (healer, trailseer, sigilist, investigator), ask the real claimant or other roles to confirm or contradict it. Push the vote onto the visitor whose claim is contradicted, unexplained, or fabricated. If a visitor was already eliminated, read their revealed role as a sign of which wolf or killer was acting through bodies. Spend a watch only when it is likely to yield a name list the town can cross-check, and keep your last watch in reserve.
situation: After a night with a death or a saved attack, the sentinel holds a private watch result naming one or more visitors at the victim's or protected player's door. The sentinel opens the day with it so the visitors must account for themselves. Information landscape: Information-rich: morning announcements confirm deaths, saves and revealed roles, and other investigative claimants may add visit reports to cross-check against the watch. Stakes: Mid-game with several threats still alive (wolves plus a lone killer). A well-timed visitor reveal can force a wolf or killer into a bad fake claim and win a day-two or day-three elimination. A mishandled or hidden one wastes a scarce watch and leaves the sentinel exposed anyway. Consensus: The village has no settled target. Everyone is waiting for evidence after the night's deaths or attack, so a concrete visitor list can set the agenda. My position: driving Heat: Minimal. The sentinel is treated as a credible source bringing concrete night data, with no one suspecting them yet. Forward exposure: Claiming sentinel and publishing the watch list is irreversible. It exposes your role and leaves you with one watch or none, which makes you a likely target for wolf kills or blocks. It also commits you to the accusation against the visitors. In exchange, it forces fast, checkable claims from them, and the contradictions that follow can expose wolves or the killer. Target landscape: The small set of players seen visiting the scene, including dead ones, whose roles are revealed, and living ones who claim healer, trailseer, sigilist or similar. Evidence is a hard watch result. Their explanations are behavioral and can be checked against other claimants. Public vs private: Privately knows exactly who visited a specific door on a specific night. The town only knows the public morning outcome (a save, or a death and role), not who visited.

action: When another player puts you in a suspect pool, or asks why you have no watch result, answer with the true mechanics: state which nights you used your two watches and that they are spent. This explains your silence and shows you have no night action left, so you are not a wolf who is hiding results. Then redirect the room to the unverified players. When you share a result, share only what helps and cannot be turned against you, and do it only after weighing how much a full sentinel reveal will make you a night-kill target.
situation: Day discussion in the mid-to-late game. A claimed investigator or other trusted claimant has cleared some players and pooled the sentinel with the remaining wolf suspects. The sentinel has to explain its role state or its night results. Information landscape: Fairly rich: investigator clears, prior healer saves or sigil outcomes, and claimed night actions. A few players remain unverified, and my own result or lack of one is being used against me. Stakes: With few players alive, a wrong vote on me or a mislynch gives the wolves or the lone killer a near-parity path. Clearing myself and pointing the vote at the right unverified player preserves town numbers. Consensus: The room leans on a claimed investigator's clears and narrows the wolf pool by elimination. It is still open to reasoned correction. My position: Holding out against inclusion in the suspect pool while steering the vote toward unverified players. Heat: Moderate to high: an investigator or other claimant has publicly grouped me with the wolf suspects over a missing night result. Forward exposure: Revealing the sentinel role and the watch count commits me to a claim others can check against the night record. It cannot be undone, and it removes any night-action threat, so wolves may see me as a lower-priority kill. Revealing live results makes me a night-kill target. Target landscape: A small pool of unverified players, including me, a quiet role such as the vigilante, and a hidden wolf, after the investigator cleared others. Reads rest on deduction from missing reports, not on hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately I know my watches are used up and what I saw on those nights; publicly, others infer from my missing report that I may be hiding something or be a wolf.

action: When several roles claim night actions on the same body or target and your watch result matches some of those claims, you can confirm that match, because it solidifies town-aligned claimants and exposes mismatches. Before you do, weigh the exposure. Name only the visitors you actually saw, and give the result at the point where it gets a mislynch redirected. If a lone killer or necromancer could still use a dead town role's body, and you are the only unprotected information role left, hold back the full reveal or ask the healer to protect you. Once you have confirmed, treat yourself as the likely kill target that night.
situation: Day discussion after a night kill or sigil strike on a wolf. Several players claim night actions on the body and the village is about to vote. Information landscape: Rich: a confirmed dead wolf, a concealed or contested kill, and several matching night-ability claims that my watch result can corroborate or contradict. Stakes: Confirming claims helps town aim its vote, but exposing the sentinel invites a night kill. If the necromancer or killer takes me, town loses its only visit-verification role. Consensus: The room is split and moving toward a vote on a player with no hard evidence. It is receptive to any confirmed information. My position: Holding out on the full reveal, ready to corroborate the matching claimants if that redirects the vote. Heat: Low from town. Threat visibility to the wolves and the lone killer rises sharply if I reveal. Forward exposure: Announcing my watch result outs me as the sentinel and cannot be taken back. It credits the matching claimants and makes me the top night target for the surviving wolf, the lone killer, or a necromancer using a fresh body. Target landscape: The room is split between an unrevealed player and a suspected illusionist. The lone killer is getting little scrutiny, and claimants on the dead wolf are not yet verified. Public vs private: Privately I saw exactly who visited the dead wolf, and several claimants' stories match it. Publicly those claims are unverified, and the room is still weighing an unrevealed player and a suspected illusionist.

action: In a four-player endgame with both watches spent, share your actual watch history in plain, rule-accurate terms: who you watched, which nights, and who visited. State that watching is itself a visit, but that you are not shown your own watch. Then say which remaining players your logs clear or leave open. Before the vote, ask the confirmed-town vigilante or healer to name one target aloud, and back that target whichever way your read leans, so town votes together. Do not leave the room split between the wolf and the lone killer, because one wrong elimination hands evil parity.
situation: Four players are left: one wolf, one lone killer and two town. The sentinel is out of watches and trusted, and town must pick the right evil player to eliminate while discussion splits between the two unclaimed suspects. Information landscape: Rich in claims, wills, dead roles and confirmed reanimated attacks, but the sentinel has no night resource left. Only historical logs and behavioral reads remain. Stakes: At four alive, one wrong elimination or a split vote lets evil reach parity, so town must unify on a single target this day. Consensus: The room is fractured between the quiet player and the aggressive questioner. Town has no single agreed target, and the claimed vigilante's shot is the swing resource. My position: Holding out or split from the vigilante's read, with no coordinated plan. Heat: None: your town alignment was confirmed by a publicly announced healer save. Forward exposure: Naming a primary suspect and repeating that you are out of watches commits you to that read in front of the vigilante. It is hard to retract, so ground it in logs and behavior and keep room to pivot if the vigilante's read differs. Target landscape: Two unclaimed players remain, one wolf and one lone killer (necromancer). One quietly deflects and the other aggressively questions late claims. There is no hard evidence, only behavior and old watch logs. Public vs private: Both watches are used up, so you have only past logs (no visitors on the watched players). Publicly you are confirmed town-aligned, so your word carries weight. Your private logs are thin but accurate.

action: When a rival claimant challenges your lack of output or your results, answer with only accurate mechanics and facts. Watching is a visit, and you do not see your own watch in your result. Give your real watch targets, nights and results, and say plainly when a result was empty. If you are unsure of a rule, state only the part you are sure of rather than inventing a rule to win the exchange. Then move on to the facts that separate the challenger from the claimed town roles. A false rule claim reads as a wolf's fabrication to the deciding town player and is not recoverable.
situation: In a four-player endgame the sentinel is challenged by a rival role claimant in a head-to-head credibility dispute, and the deciding town player votes on whose mechanics sound true. Information landscape: Rich in revealed dead roles, a confirmed vigilante shot and claim histories, so any statement that contradicts the rules is caught and read as a lie. Stakes: With four alive and one wolf left, the vote on the sentinel decides the game. A single credibility-destroying error gives the wolf parity. Consensus: The room is still forming, and the deciding confirmed vigilante is judging claim credibility on mechanical accuracy. My position: Holding out under pressure, defending a claim against a direct challenger. Heat: High: the rival claimant openly questions your lack of output and your authenticity. Forward exposure: Any rule statement goes on the permanent public record and a confirmed town player can check it against the rules at once. A false mechanical claim cannot be taken back. An accurate statement costs little. Target landscape: The room is choosing between the rival claimant (trailseer), a quiet neutral and you. The evidence is a clash of role claims with no hard proof. Public vs private: You privately know you did watch the neutral player, but a rival claimant is pressing you. Your public statement can turn a manageable credibility challenge into an apparent wolf lie.

action: If you are the Sentinel and your watch result is null (no visitors) or names no one suspicious, keep the role hidden. Contribute through behavioral reads and vote analysis, such as pointing at players who are silent or inconsistent, and do not announce that you are a night-information role. Claim only if (a) your watch caught a visitor you can name as an actionable lead, (b) you are about to be voted out and need to prove you are Town, or (c) a confirmed Town role needs corroboration. In those cases, claim with the concrete result and keep your remaining watch in reserve. A null result on an unpressured player adds little but makes you a high-priority night kill.
situation: Day 2 follows night deaths of Town power roles. A claimed investigator has shared a result and the room is info-starved. The Sentinel is tempted to volunteer a role claim with a null or low-value watch result, although nobody has asked for it. Information landscape: Information-starved. Town power roles died at night, claims are unverified, and no evil visits have been caught. The only hard data is a claimed check and the Sentinel's private null watch. Stakes: Several killers are still active and Town has already lost key roles. Losing the Sentinel's remaining watch to a night kill costs Town a scarce information source for nothing. There is time to wait for a result that can actually shift a vote. Consensus: The room is loosely aligned and drifting toward abstaining or a low-information vote. Nobody is demanding claims, and the shared reads come only from talk. My position: Driving the discussion in the open, with the option of staying with the majority. Heat: None. The Sentinel is unsuspected and could volunteer information without anyone asking for it. Forward exposure: A role claim is irreversible. It tells the wolves and the lone killer which seat holds a watching role. A null result gives the village almost nothing in return, and the claim can be used for night targeting. Staying quiet keeps the claim available for a later, higher-value moment. Target landscape: The pool is the quiet or inactive players. There are no caught visitors and no confirmed evil, so the basis is behavioral only. A claimed investigator may have cleared one player, which leaves few hard leads. Public vs private: Privately holding a watch result of no visitors on an unpressured target. Publicly, nobody is accusing that target or asking the Sentinel for information, so the result would not change the room's read.

action: On Day 1, with no deaths and no vote, take part in the opening round with light, sincere content. Ask questions, comment on tone and on who claims or avoids claiming, and set out a simple plan for the first nights. Do not claim Sentinel and do not volunteer role details. Do not go fully silent, because the quietest seat can look like a safe, low-value kill. Treat the night kill as largely random and do not over-invest in disguise, and save the watch for a night when a visit is likely to be informative.
situation: Day 1 discussion with nobody dead or claimed and no vote scheduled. The Sentinel, holding both watches, must decide how visible to be before the first night. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are no night actions, deaths, claims or reads. Stakes: Nothing is close to a tipping point on Day 1. Early survival of an information role matters, but the first-night kill is mostly arbitrary, so avoid over-optimizing for it and avoid giving the wolves a reason to pick this seat. Consensus: No consensus exists. The room is feeling out positions in an opening round with no vote at stake. My position: With the majority, staying low-key and neither driving nor holding out. Heat: None. Day 1 has no accusations and no vote. Forward exposure: A role claim now would reveal a watcher with no results to show and would be irreversible. Light talk reveals nothing and can be changed later. Complete silence costs little in the discussion but can make the player look like the easiest kill. Target landscape: All nine other players are unknown. There are no behavioral reads, no claims and no night data. Public vs private: Privately holding the Sentinel role with both watches unused. Publicly, no roles, claims or reads exist yet, so there is nothing to confirm or contradict.

action: When your own watch result places a player at a night-one death scene, report it plainly and vote to eliminate that visitor, especially if they deny any visit and have no role claim. Hard evidence only you hold outweighs a retaliatory fabrication accusation. Check first that no other role could explain the visit, such as a healer or a claimed investigator. If other visitors are listed, weigh each against the claims before committing.
situation: After a night-one kill, you watched the victim's door and caught a visitor. The visitor denies visiting and accuses you of faking the result to force a mislynch. Information landscape: Information-rich: your own watch result, confirmed dead roles, and a claimed investigator's check all point the same way. Stakes: Removing a night-immune lone killer or a wolf on day two preserves the town's numbers and removes a nightly kill. A wrong vote shrinks the buffer. This is a high-leverage day. Consensus: The room is nearly aligned behind your report, since the evidence is concrete and corroborated by a claimed investigator's read on another player. The accused is isolated. My position: Driving the vote with your own evidence. Heat: Near zero from the room. Only the accused tries to cast doubt on you, and their retaliatory vote is the only suspicion against you. Forward exposure: Voting on the watch result commits you permanently to your sentinel claim and makes you a likely night target for the surviving evil. The public vote cannot be undone. If the flip shows town, your credibility collapses. Target landscape: The caught visitor has no role claim and offers only a flat denial plus a counter-accusation against you. The alternatives are abstaining or pressuring unaccused town members who have no evidence against them. The visitor is the only candidate backed by hard evidence. Public vs private: You privately hold a watch result showing the accused visited the dead player, which contradicts their public claim of never visiting anyone. The room has only your word, and the accused calls it fabricated.

action: Before voting against a claimed town power role over a mechanical slip, check the claim against the rules and your own results. If you were roleblocked, a Chanteuse is alive, so a claim that someone cannot be blocked without being evil is a rules misunderstanding, not proof of evil. Treat a confused claim as weak evidence. Use your vote on a target backed by hard evidence, such as a caught visitor, a confirmed guilty check, or a voting-record contradiction. If no such target exists, abstain when allowed or place the vote on the best evidence-backed suspect, and state plainly why a mechanics error alone does not justify the elimination.
situation: A claiming town power role fumbles a mechanic while accusing another claimant. The room piles on, calling the claim fabricated, and you are trusted enough that your vote can tip it. Information landscape: Information-rich on the dead and claims, but no hard evidence against the accused. The case rests on a confused statement. Stakes: Both evil factions are still alive. Wasting a vote on a town power role shrinks the buffer and removes an ability, which accelerates a town loss. Consensus: The room is heavily aligned against the confused claimant, driven by a behavioral and mechanical-error argument rather than any hard result. My position: With the majority, having joined the formal accusation. Heat: None. You are trusted as the sentinel after your earlier watch result was validated by a dead player's flip. Forward exposure: Joining the accusation aligns you with the majority and leaves you accountable when the flip reveals town. A vote cast cannot be reversed, and losing a power role costs both its ability and a body of town numbers. Target landscape: The main candidate is a claimed sigilist under scrutiny for confusion over roleblock mechanics. The alternatives are the suspected lone killer, whom a dead illusionist targeted earlier, and other claimants. The case against the sigilist rests on behavior, not on evidence. Public vs private: You privately know you were roleblocked, so a Chanteuse is active. The sigilist's claim is mechanically confused but you have no private evidence that they are evil. The room reads the confusion as fabrication.

action: In a four-player endgame where a rival claimant's story is contradicted by your own watch result, state the watch result in discussion before the vote. Name the night you watched and who actually visited you, and show that the rival's claim does not match. Then cast your vote on that contradicted claimant, not on a silent bystander. Keep your vote on the liar even if the room is already against you. A vote on a third player gives the confirmed town player no reason to switch and lets the liar's framing pass unchallenged.
situation: The sentinel is in a direct credibility clash with a wolf-aligned counter-claimant at four players. A wrong vote or a lost vote ends Town's majority. Information landscape: Information-rich. Several dead roles are confirmed, voting records are public, and the sentinel holds a private watch result that falsifies the rival's tracking story. Stakes: One lost vote leaves three players, and the following night kill hands the wolves parity. The sentinel's vote and credibility are the last lever Town has. Consensus: The room is lining up against the sentinel on the strength of the rival's counter-claim. Nobody is testing that claim against the records. My position: Holding out alone against the forming majority. Heat: Extreme. The confirmed town player and the room treat the sentinel as guilty after an apparent rules contradiction. Forward exposure: The vote is terminal and cannot be undone. Spending it on a third player abandons any chance of persuading the confirmed town player. Revealing the watch result commits the sentinel to a checkable claim, but it is the only route to flipping the room. Target landscape: Three living suspects: a quiet player who has not claimed, a rival claimant who fabricated results and framed the sentinel, and the sentinel itself. The claimant is the only one with a verifiable lie against the sentinel's private record. The quiet player is judged on behavior alone. Public vs private: Privately the sentinel holds watch evidence that the rival claimant fabricated their tracking story. Publicly the room reads the sentinel as the liar because of a perceived contradiction.

action: At four players with both a wolf and a lone killer alive, work out the board before the vote. For each candidate elimination, count who is left after the night kill and whether the wolves or the lone killer then win. Share that count openly in discussion and agree one target with the confirmed town player before voting. If you cannot persuade them, do not cast a lone vote on a different player. A lone vote only splits Town and lets the plurality pick the wrong elimination. Join the confirmed town ally's target unless your own watch evidence directly contradicts it. If it does, reveal that evidence first.
situation: Four players remain: a claiming vigilante, the sentinel, a lone killer and a suspected wolf. Town is split between two eliminations and each one carries a different parity risk. Information landscape: Information-rich. Confirmed town roles, public voting records and reanimated kill history are available. The sentinel's watches are exhausted. Stakes: Removing the lone killer while a wolf lives lets that wolf reach parity on the next night kill. The vote decides which evil faction survives, so a split town vote wastes the one elimination Town has. Consensus: The confirmed town player is pushing the lone killer. The sentinel prefers the quiet suspected wolf. No shared plan for handling the parity math exists. My position: Holding out alone for a different target than the town ally. Heat: Low. Discussion centers on the two unclaimed players, not the sentinel. Forward exposure: A solitary dissenting vote is public and permanent. It isolates the sentinel from the confirmed town player and cannot be taken back. A plurality can then remove the wrong evil faction and let the wolf win at night. Target landscape: Two unclaimed players: a probable lone killer shown by reanimated kills, and a quiet survivor suspected to be the last wolf. The case against the quiet player rests on voting-record behavior. The case against the killer rests on kill history. Public vs private: The sentinel has no fresh visit records because its watches are used up. It relies on public voting history, such as the target having voted against the sentinel earlier, and no private fact contradicts the public read.

action: When a hard role counter-claim erupts and your own watch result bears on one claimant, treat a visit you observed as evidence of an action, not of the role claimed. Ask what the claimed role's ability would actually require. A visit fits an attack, a block, a sigil or any other visit-based ability. Check the claimant's story against the rules (e.g., an investigator's check is a visit, but so is a wolf's kill). If the room has converged on one claimant and your private data does not clearly contradict that consensus, vote with the consensus rather than defending the claimant you saw visit. If your watch placed a claimant at a dead player's door, count that as damaging to them, not as a vindication.
situation: A hard 1-for-1 role counter-claim has formed. The village is uniting against one claimant, and the sentinel's private watch data about a visit is being misread, leading it to vote against the town consensus. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths with revealed roles, a healer save, a watch report of who visited whom, and an exclusive-role conflict. The weak point is interpreting what a visit actually proves. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive. Your single vote is not decisive, since the majority outvotes you either way, but a dissent vote spends your credibility and shields a killer or wolf from the rest of the town. The cost is in trust, not in the immediate tally. Consensus: The village is closely aligned on eliminating one claimant, based on the counter-claim logic and your own watch report. My position: holding out Heat: Very low. You are trusted as the Sentinel through a confirmed save or a watch result that drove the day's lead, so you are not under suspicion. Forward exposure: A vote against the room's consensus is public and permanent. It marks your record as aligned with whichever side that claimant belongs to. If the claimant flips as wolf or killer, you are exposed as having defended them. It cannot be retracted. Target landscape: Two claimants contest one exclusive role (investigator or sigilist). One is a real Town role and the other is a wolf or killer fabricating a claim. The evidence is a night visit seen by you plus the claimants' own statements, with the room's consensus already formed. Public vs private: You privately saw a claimant's visit at a night door. The town reads that visit as a tell, or as ambiguous. You are tempted to read it as supporting the claimant's cover story, though a visit is equally consistent with a wolf or killer attack.

action: On Night 1, with no claims, deaths or reads, spend one watch rather than hold both. Pick a quiet player who has not drawn attention and is not obviously the room's focus. A door that gets visited gives hard evidence: a visitor who dies in the night is a verified role, and a visitor who turns out to be a killer is a lead. Hold the second watch back. Accept that about half the time the result is empty, because the watch can be blocked or you can be killed first. This is a policy over many games, not a bet on one door.
situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1. The sentinel must decide whether to commit one of two lifetime watches blind or conserve both. Past results were a mixed bag: the lone killer caught at a door, a trailseer or healer visit verified, three visitors at once, empty doors, and the sentinel itself killed or blocked that same night. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths, no claims, no checks and no votes. Any target is a speculative probe. Stakes: The board is wide open and no single result decides the game. A watch is cheap here, but half of the sentinel's lifetime capacity is spent on a blind pick. The sentinel is also a likely early wolf or lone-killer kill, so a result may never be delivered. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unverified, separated only by Day 1 behavior. A quiet, unpressured player is a reasonable default door because there is no evidence to rank the others.

action: On Day 2, share the Night 1 watch result only if it names at least one visitor. Give the visitor names and cross-check them against the morning deaths and any claims, since a visitor who died overnight verifies their own role. If a visit points at a player who is likely the lone killer or a wolf, push that name for the vote. If the result was zero visitors, or you cannot cross-check it, keep your role private for now and use it only to sharpen your reads. Claiming with an empty result gave the wolves a target and let the Chanteuse block you without giving the town anything.
situation: Day 2 after a Night 1 watch. The sentinel holds a private result and must decide whether to reveal the role and the visitor list. Revealing can verify other roles or catch a killer, but it exposes the sentinel to the wolves' night kill and to Chanteuse blocks. Information landscape: One private visit result plus the morning report. It becomes information-rich only if the visitor names can be matched to deaths or claims. Stakes: A named visitor who matches a night death or claim can lead to a killer being voted out early. An unsupported claim only paints a target on the sentinel. Target landscape: Living players who may have visited your Night 1 door, plus players who claim roles on Day 2. A visitor who died overnight and was revealed is verified. Other visitors are only leads and need cross-checking against claims. Remember that a failed wolf attack on a night-immune target looks like a visit and can be disguised as an investigative check.

action: Keep the final watch until there is a concrete reason to look at a specific door. Good reasons are a claimed role the wolves are likely to attack, a contested claimant whose night activity could be tested, or a suspect your own results and the public record already point to. Do not spend it on a player picked only because they voted against or accused you, since that is a behavioral grudge and not a lead. If nothing qualifies this night, hold the watch and re-evaluate next night.
situation: Mid-game with one watch left, after the sentinel was revealed. A player voted alone against the sentinel, and the sentinel watched that accuser. The result was zero visitors and the final watch was gone. The sentinel then had no ability for the rest of the game and died on Night 3. Information landscape: Still thin. The claims and visit reports on Day 2 are unverified and the vote ended in abstention. There are no hard alignments, so any target comes from behavior only. Stakes: The last watch is the sentinel's only remaining ability. Spending it on a door with no evidence behind it leaves the sentinel powerless while the killers keep acting. Target landscape: The living players after Night 1. A lone accuser or vocal adversary is a weak target with no evidence behind the pick. A likely kill target or a claimant in a role conflict is a stronger door.

action: Spend the last watch on a player who is likely to receive a night visit. Good candidates are a contested claimed power role (investigator, sigilist, trailseer) whose claim others dispute, or a claimed informational role the wolves would want to kill. Visitors reveal a claim's truth, because a real investigator or sigilist will show up at the door they say they used. A watch on a quiet suspect or a cleared player only returns "no visitors", since killers visit their victims and not themselves. If the target is attacked, the visitor list names the visitors, or a body concealed by an illusionist tells you wolves struck. Tell the town what you saw, and do it in a form that survives your own death.
situation: Day 2-3 ended in an abstain or tied vote after conflicting role claims. The sentinel holds one watch and must decide where to place it for the night. Information landscape: Information-rich on claims: counter-claims, a trailseer report, a cleared player and sigil declarations. Little hard evidence on who is wolf, so the watch is the only way to test claims against actual visits. Stakes: This is the sentinel's final watch, and the mid-game board has several competing claimants. A wasted watch leaves Town with no visit-tracking for the rest of the game. A well-placed one can corroborate or refute a key claim before the next vote. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, healer, trailseer and sigilist, with the contested claimant under suspicion and likely to be visited. Also quiet or tied-vote suspects and players already cleared by the investigator. The likely-visited players give a real chance of visitor data. The suspects and cleared players give almost none.

action: If you have publicly claimed sentinel and are the obvious wolf target, still place the final watch only where a visit is likely, such as a contested claimant or a probable wolf kill target. Do not spend it on a quiet or already-cleared player just to use it. If no candidate is both contested and likely to be visited, keep the watch in reserve for a later night, because a held watch costs nothing. Make sure what you learn can be passed on by claim before you can be killed.
situation: The sentinel has publicly claimed and is exposed as a night target. They are tempted to burn the last watch on a low-information player. Spent that way it returned zero visits, and the sentinel was killed or nearly killed anyway. Information landscape: Many claims are public, but the available targets give no actionable lead. Prior watches or checks have not produced a concrete suspect. Stakes: Town has a buffer, but losing the sentinel and its last watch would remove the visit-tracking tool. Wasting the watch on a no-lead target buys nothing. Target landscape: Investigator-cleared players and quiet unvetted players, who are low-yield. Contested claimants and likely wolf targets are high-yield. The choice is between spending the watch now and holding it for a later night when a lead exists.

action: When a claimed Sentinel or Trailseer names you as the visitor to a night victim, do not flatly deny it, and do not claim a visiting role (such as Sigilist) whose real holder is alive and can counter-claim at once. Both approaches lost on Day 2 by 1-for-1 contradiction. First check which visit-capable Town roles (Healer, Sigilist, Investigator, Trailseer) are already dead or unclaimed. Claim a visit-role only if its holder cannot contradict you, for example because the holder died with the role hidden by the Illusionist. If every available claim can be countered, do not stake your life on a binary duel. Concede only that a visit occurred and argue that visits are not kills, since many Town roles visit. Then move the vote toward another suspect, using the Trailseer's tracked target, a wolf-looking player, or an unclaimed role. The aim is to split the village's votes so no majority forms on you, because the Day 2 vote is the only way you can be removed.
situation: Day 2 discussion after Night 1. A claimed Sentinel (or Trailseer) publicly reports the Serial Killer as the visitor to the night victim. The SK must survive the coming vote with no night immunity against a vote. Information landscape: Information-rich. The victim's role is revealed, and the Sentinel and Trailseer have reported specific visit results. The village can cross-check claims for contradictions. Stakes: The Day 2 vote can end the Serial Killer's game outright, and the SK cannot be killed at night. A majority against me means immediate elimination, so the whole game turns on preventing a majority. Consensus: The village is converging on me. Players point out the contradiction between the Sentinel's report and my denial or fake claim, and the evidence is concrete rather than behavioral. My position: holding out against a forming majority Heat: Maximum. I was named as the visitor to the player the Serial Killer killed on Night 1, based on a concrete night result. Forward exposure: Claiming a role with limited charges, or a unique role, commits me to a truth-versus-lie clash with the real holder and cannot be undone. A flat denial commits me to calling a verified-looking report false, with no fallback. A non-committal framing plus redirected suspicion keeps retreat options open. Target landscape: The accuser (a claimed Sentinel or Trailseer) holds a direct visit report. Living Town role holders could counter any fake claim. Other suspects, such as unclaimed players or those the Trailseer tracked, have only behavioral or weak evidence against them. Public vs private: Privately I know the named visit was my own night kill. Publicly a claimed Sentinel or Trailseer has accurately reported it, and the room treats that report as hard evidence.

action: When heat on you is high and the room is split or leaning toward you, don't just defend. Name the other contested suspect, usually the surviving wolf or a player with a bad vote record, and build a concrete case from public facts: who voted with whom, who protected a dead wolf, who dodged a claim. Spell out the vote you want ("vote X, not me") and address the undecided or neutral voters directly, since they decide a close vote. If a verifiable immunity or mechanical result is already public and the room has consolidated, don't call it a lie. Concede nothing about your role, and use the remaining time to turn the room's attention onto the wolf. A passive rationalization like "I was waiting for info" gives the room nothing to switch to.
situation: A mid-game day with few players alive after the night deaths. A dead sentinel, a dead wolf, or a claimed vigilante or sigilist result has put the room's attention on me. The vote is imminent and I can only be removed by a daytime vote, so I need the room to vote someone else out. Information landscape: Information-rich. Revealed dead roles, public vote records, and claimed night results narrow the pool of suspects and make a bare denial look weak. Stakes: With about five players alive, one vote can end my game, and my immunity does not help against a daytime vote. I survive only if the room splits or redirects before the ballot, so the vote on me is the one decision that matters. Consensus: The village and the surviving wolf are coalescing against me because I am the easiest or best-supported target. Where a competing suspect exists, the room is split and one or two swing voters decide the outcome. My position: Holding out against a forming or overwhelming consensus, with no allies who aren't also a threat. Heat: High to extreme. The room is accusing me over passivity, a dead wolf's vote on me, or a claimed result suggesting immunity. Forward exposure: Accusing another player commits me to a visible case that I can pivot from if the target is cleared. Calling a claimed mechanical result a lie, or giving a bare passive defense, leaves no way to retreat and no alternative target. A concrete case against the wolf can be reversed, while a flat denial of hard evidence cannot. Target landscape: The choice is between me and one or two other suspects, usually the surviving wolf or an unconfirmed player with a questionable vote. Evidence is mostly vote records, claims, and dead players' wills, with no hard proof against anyone but me. Undecided voters such as a speculator or neutral hold the deciding votes. Public vs private: Privately I am the night-immune serial killer, and I may have killed the dead player the room is using against me. Publicly I am a quiet or accused player who needs the room to see someone else as the bigger threat.

action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer publicly places you at the Night 1 kill and the room is converging on you, spend the pre-vote discussion and your last word rebuilding doubt in that report. Say a visit shows presence, not guilt. Point to the other visitor or suspect with the most public evidence, such as the player the Trailseer tracked visiting a wolf victim or the investigator, and ask for the vote to go there. At the vote, put your ballot on that alternative target. Do not use it on a lone counter-vote against the accuser or a counter-claimer, because that gains nothing and confirms the 1-vs-all duel. If you fake-claim a visiting role, first check that the real holder is not alive and likely to counter-claim. Pick a claim whose visit pattern fits the report. You can only be removed by a vote and you are immune at night, so the aim is to split the room, force a tie, or draw abstentions before the ballot, not to win a duel.
situation: Day 2 vote. Night 1 produced a kill, and a Sentinel, or similar, claims to have seen the Serial Killer visit the victim. The room is pushing to eliminate me, and I must choose between a retaliatory vote on the accuser and a different play. Information landscape: Information-rich. There is a role-confirmed kill, a specific visitor report, and a second tracking or investigation result clearing or implicating other players, so my lies are easy to test. Stakes: Eliminating me ends the Serial Killer win condition at once. As the only unkillable-at-night evil, I can lose only by vote, so this one vote determines whether I survive past Day 2. Consensus: The village and the wolves are near-unanimous against me, on the strength of one specific visit report. Only the neutral player hesitates or abstains. My position: Holding out alone against a forming dogpile. Heat: Critical. A town investigative role has named me as a visitor to the Night 1 victim, and the table, wolves included, is moving to eliminate me on Day 2. Forward exposure: A lone vote against the accuser or counter-claimer commits me to a zero-sum duel against a credible town role. It cannot be undone and gives no coalition path. Voting on a third suspect, or pushing for abstention or a tie, keeps my position flexible and does not stake my role on one claim. Target landscape: The candidates are the accusing Sentinel (an unverified claim, but accurate), any counter-claimer to my fake role (probably the real holder), and a third suspect such as the player the Trailseer saw visiting a victim. The accuser has the strongest evidence. The third suspect is the only target that lets me look aligned with the room. Public vs private: Privately I am the Serial Killer who made the Night 1 kill. Publicly a town informational role has accurately placed me at the victim's door, and my denial or fake claim is the only thing contradicting it.

action: When a claimed information role (e.g. the Investigator) has publicly cleared you or never suspected you, and a day vote or accusation has singled out another player, stab that singled-out player. If the investigator's accusation is the only strong lead, kill their target. A death that reveals a wolf validates the investigator, keeps your clearance intact, and shifts the next day's momentum onto the remaining wolf instead of you. If two targets are pressed, prefer the one drawing a consistent push from several voters over the one with a single isolated accuser.
situation: Night after an inconclusive day vote. A claimed investigator has publicly pushed one player and voted against them, while you sit as an unsuspected or cleared lone killer. You choose a night kill that can ride the town's existing momentum. Information landscape: Information-rich: public role claims, a day vote record, and a claimed favorable check on you, but no verified roles besides announced deaths. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil players alive and no one close to winning. The kill is useful for thinning wolves and protecting your clearance, but one kill does not decide the game. The main risk is losing your cover, not an immediate swing. Forward exposure: The kill leaves a visible stab mark, so the village knows a lone killer is active, but it does not identify you. It is irreversible. A Sentinel watch or Trailseer track on the victim could show your visit, so favor a target the room is already focused on. Your cleared status makes you an unlikely suspect. Target landscape: The player the claimed investigator singled out and voted against, vocal players pushing counter-lynches, and the claimed information roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Sigilist, Trailseer). Choice rests on public vote records and claimed results, not on verified roles.

action: When the only player who voted against you (or broke an abstain consensus to target you) is the clearest hostile voter, stab them, since that is the most likely wolf. Before doing so, check whether a second candidate is under pressure from a credible claimed info role, and prefer that player if there is one. If your accuser is the only strong target, accept the kill but expect the town to read it as retaliation. At the next day's discussion, point to the victim's revealed wolf role and your lack of any other motive, and push the room toward the surviving wolf.
situation: After a sparse day vote (often an abstain or near-abstain) where exactly one player voted to eliminate you, you decide on the night kill. Retaliating against the accuser removes a likely wolf, but it can make you the most suspicious survivor. Information landscape: Information-rich on claims and the vote record, but without verified roles. The accuser's alignment is inferred from a single vote. Stakes: Early-mid game, and you are already a named target of a wolf. Removing an accuser trims the pack, but a misread retaliation narrative can get you voted out the next day. The kill is a bounded-risk policy whose misses are priced in. Forward exposure: Killing your lone accuser creates an obvious retaliation narrative: once their role is revealed, their earlier vote against you becomes evidence that you are an opposing threat. It cannot be undone after the morning report. Whether this hurts depends on how the town reads a dead wolf's vote against you. Target landscape: The sole voter against you, claimed info roles (Trailseer, Sigilist, Sentinel, Investigator), and quiet unverified players. The accuser's evidence is behavioral only, a vote that may come from a wolf trying to remove the SK or from a confused villager.

action: When the healer's protection pattern is publicly visible (an announced save last morning, or a claimed investigator who just outed a wolf and is the obvious protect target), shift the night kill to a different high-value target. Pick the claimed sentinel, trailseer, vigilante or sigilist, or a quiet unconfirmed player who is likely a power role. If the healer must protect another player and cannot cover the investigator and the new target in the same night, the kill lands. The healer can never protect itself, so if you can narrow down the healer, kill the healer. If you have no read on the healer, attack the next most dangerous town role, not the one the town already treats as protected.
situation: Late-game after the wolves have fallen or been thinned. A claimed investigator has a verified finding and a healer save on them has just been announced. As the lone killer you must choose a night kill among several surviving town power roles while the healer is almost certainly still guarding that investigator. Information landscape: Information-rich: a wolf flip confirmed the investigator's claim, and the Game Master announced a healer save on the investigator. The healer's identity is still unknown, but the protection habit is public. Stakes: With about five players left and the serial killer needing at most one other alive, every wasted night costs a day of progress. The town's voting bloc is still intact and can vote you out, so a blocked kill leaves four town power roles alive and pressure on you. Each night must convert into a death. Forward exposure: A kill on a non-obvious target is a secret strike that reveals only the death and role, with no link to you. A failed attack on the saved investigator would be announced publicly and confirm the healer, so the choice cannot be undone once the night resolves. Picking an unexpected target keeps the healer guessing and avoids a wasted night. Target landscape: The publicly saved or wolf-convicting claimed investigator (likely re-protected), the claimed sentinel or other power roles, and quiet unconfirmed players who may be the healer. The saved investigator is the obvious healer target; the rest are less predictable. Evidence is the public save announcement and the wolf flip, not behavior.

action: When a claimed Town role (investigator, sentinel) has produced a result and the room is split on whether to trust it, add your own verifiable night facts and the rules that bear on them to back the accurate claim. State which player you placed a sigil on and that it had no effect, and explain that a non-trigger only means the target did not attack, so it neither clears nor convicts them. Also state that checks, watches and protections count as visits but are not attacks, so they never trigger a sigil. If a claimant's story contradicts these mechanics, or two players counter-claim the same unique role, point to that contradiction and urge a vote on it. Disclose the sigil placement once it is spent and your role is no longer needed for future nights. While you still hold a sigil, weigh the exposure cost before revealing.
situation: A Town claimant (investigator or sentinel) has made a claim, an accused player or rival claimant is pushing back, and the sigilist has relevant night-action facts that either corroborate the claim or expose a mechanical contradiction. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced healer saves, claimed check results, a known sigil placement, and counter-claims that can be tested against the rules. Stakes: A mid-game vote can remove an active wolf and its roleblock or kill capability. The village has room to correct a mistake but not many wasted days. A fabricated-conspiracy narrative left unanswered could split Town. Consensus: The village is leaning toward one claimant because of a healer-confirmed save or a mechanical contradiction, but is still open to a counter-narrative of fabricated coordination. My position: Driving alongside or with the majority by corroborating the better-supported claimant. Heat: Low. The only pressure is verbal retaliation or collusion accusations from the accused player, with no vote-based suspicion on the sigilist. Forward exposure: Claiming sigilist and naming the target commits the agent publicly and cannot be undone. It reveals that a sigil is spent, and wolves can then target the role. The cost is low once sigils are exhausted or only one remains. Target landscape: A player accused by a claimed investigator, or two investigator counter-claimants, set against a Town claimant backed by hard public evidence such as an announced healer save. Candidates are judged on mechanical consistency plus announced facts, not tone. Public vs private: Privately knows exactly where sigils were placed and that they did not trigger. The public only has competing claims and an accused player's counter-narrative, so the sigilist's account is a hidden, checkable data point.

action: While you still hold sigils and are not under suspicion, keep the sigilist role hidden. Confirm only what helps Town, such as a claimed investigator's clean result on you, and steer discussion toward the hard evidence (a sentinel's visitor catch, an announced save, a body). This keeps kill priority off you and preserves the sigils for later nights. Reveal the role only if you are pressed or your sigil facts are needed to settle a vote. If you do reveal, give a short account of what was placed and what the sigil result meant.
situation: Early in the game, with sigils unspent, hard evidence (a dead wolf, a sentinel catch, an investigator clear) points at one suspect. The sigilist is cleared or unnoticed and has no urgent need to reveal. Information landscape: Information-rich: a corpse with a revealed role, a claimed visit catch, and an investigator check on the sigilist. Stakes: An early vote on a caught visitor can remove a killer and halve night deaths. Keeping the sigilist alive and unrevealed preserves both sigils for the late game. Consensus: The room is converging on the hard-evidence claim with little dissent. My position: With the majority, reinforcing the evidence-based read. Heat: None. The agent is cleared or ignored and is not a suspect. Forward exposure: Staying quiet commits to nothing and can be reversed at any time by claiming. The cost is that the agent's night facts are not available to Town until it speaks. Target landscape: A visitor caught by a claimed sentinel and claiming to be framed, versus a claimed sentinel backed by hard visit information. The decision rests on evidence, not tone. Public vs private: Town sees a cleared, cooperative player. Privately the agent holds the sigilist role with its sigils intact, which wolves would want to know about.

action: When another claimed night-role (Sentinel, Trailseer, Healer) publicly reports a visit or no-visit that involves you, corroborate the factual part truthfully and briefly. Confirm only what the report says about your own visit, e.g. 'I visited X and nothing happened' or 'I made no visit'. If you were roleblocked, you may leave that out. If your sigil produced a null result on a night victim or a visited target, report that result openly and say plainly that a null result proves nothing about your alignment. Say the remaining sigil is held in reserve. This joins the verified-visit web, lowers suspicion, and steers the room toward an abstain or toward the investigative claimants. Reveal the Sigilist role only if the corroboration needs it and a stronger investigative claimant is already drawing the night kill. Otherwise confirm the visit and keep the role private.
situation: Early day (Day 2) after a quiet or low-information night. One or two night deaths, possibly with a concealed role. Claimed Sentinel or Trailseer reports mention your visit or your absence of visits, and the village is deciding whether to abstain or chase quiet players. Information landscape: Mostly claims from night roles that intersect on shared targets. There are no confirmed guilty findings and no caught lies, so the evidence is thin and only the Sentinel/Trailseer/Healer reports overlap. Stakes: Mid-early game with a comfortable town margin. No single vote or kill decides the game, but losing the Sigilist before both sigils are used wastes its deterrent, and keeping the village aligned and abstaining protects town. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned on abstaining or on discussing the claimed investigators' reports. The basis is cross-corroborated claims and the lack of hard evidence. My position: with majority Heat: Low. You are named as a visitor or cleared by a tracker, but nobody accuses you of attacking anyone. Forward exposure: Claiming Sigilist is irreversible and exposes the role to a wolf kill or roleblock while a sigil is still unspent. Confirming only the visit and withholding the role is cheap and reversible. In both cases the remaining sigil stays hidden. Target landscape: No confirmed guilty suspect. The candidates are the claimed Sentinel, Trailseer, Healer, the quiet or unaligned visitors named in the reports, and a concealed or unrevealed victim. All the evidence is unverified claims, with no caught lies. Public vs private: Privately you know your own night visit and its sigil result (or that you were blocked). The public holds a claimed Sentinel or Trailseer report that matches or clears you. Your private knowledge confirms the public read.

action: With sigils spent and 3-4 players alive, drive the final vote openly from verified public facts: announced wills, the dead's roles, the voting record, and any Trailseer or Investigator report that matches what you know. Say plainly that your sigils are spent, so your sigil results and your own non-visits can corroborate or refute others' claims. Use sigil mechanics to rebut defenses. A 'no effect' sigil on a night attacker means night immunity (Serial Killer), not innocence. Name the one player whose story clashes with the hard evidence and ask the other town-aligned players to vote with you. Before locking in, count which evil factions are still alive.
