If both a wolf and a lone killer remain, check that eliminating your target does not leave the other killer able to finish the game, for example a Necromancer using a dead Vigilante's body. If the evidence points to one faction, commit fully.
situation: Endgame with 3-4 alive and parity close. The Sigilist is trusted and out of sigils, and must adjudicate the final vote between a counter-claiming suspect (wolf, Serial Killer, or Necromancer) and trusted town reporters. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced wills, revealed roles of the dead, public voting records, and Trailseer or Investigator reports narrow the identity of the remaining evil player. Stakes: Every vote is decisive. One wrong elimination hands the evil side parity or a win, and there are no further nights to recover. The whole game rides on getting this day's vote right. Consensus: The remaining players are small in number and broadly willing to follow a trusted evidence-based read. They align once a clear, checkable explanation is given. My position: driving Heat: Little or none. A spent power role with a consistent public record, often visible through an announced sigil strike, is trusted as confirmed town. Forward exposure: A public, irreversible commitment to one accusation, backed by the record. Safe because no sigils or night actions remain to expose. The risk is that it fixes the village on one target, leaving little room to correct if the other evil faction is the real threat. Target landscape: A few remaining players: confirmed or cleared town (by wills, a Trailseer report, or an Investigator check), a quiet unconfirmed player, and one accused claimant whose claim lacks logs or conflicts with the record. The choice rests on the evidence, not on tone. Public vs private: Private information is exhausted: both sigils are spent, so what you know is mostly your own non-visits and sigil results. These confirm or refute others' claims and the public read, and they add no hidden evidence.

action: When the room is converging on a quiet, unclaimed player and you have no private evidence against them, do not just join the pile-on. Before voting, ask the quiet player to state their role and any night results, and ask the Investigator, Sentinel and Trailseer to say whether they have checked or tracked them. Quiet players with no claims have repeatedly turned out to be Town power roles (Vigilante) or neutrals (Fortune Teller), and removing them cost the town a shooter or its margin. If a cleared pool exists, vote among the unclaimed players outside it, and prefer the one with concrete evidence: a sigil that failed to trigger on a night an attack was expected, a tracked visit, or a contradicting claim. If no such evidence exists, vote for the candidate who has the most evidence against them rather than the quietest one. If the village needs a kill and you hold a sigil, state publicly that the sigil is available and offer to place it on the suspect, so the vote is not the only tool.
situation: Mid-to-late game day vote. Some evil has been removed, and the village is converging on a quiet, unclaimed player on behavioral grounds. The sigilist is trusted and has no private evidence on the target. Information landscape: Mixed: confirmed roles and cleared players exist, and some night reports are public, but there is no hard evidence about the quiet player or the remaining evil roles. Stakes: With few players left and a lone killer or necromancer possibly alive, each wrong elimination removes a town ability or the margin for error, and hands a hidden killer a body to use or an easier path to parity. Consensus: The village is aligning on the quiet player through momentum and process of elimination, not through evidence. Confirmed roles are not unanimous. My position: with_majority Heat: Near zero. The agent is treated as confirmed town because of an announced sigil strike or corroborating reports from other town roles. Forward exposure: The vote is public, permanent and irreversible. If the target is a Town role, the village loses an ability, and a dead Vigilante body hands a Necromancer free shots. Voting with the majority costs the agent no heat, but it commits the agent to the outcome. Target landscape: A quiet, unclaimed player with no night claims, set against one or two other unverified players. Only behavioral reads exist (silence, tracked no-visit nights), with no hard evidence, and the confirmed or cleared core (Investigator, Sentinel, Healer) is not in the pool. Public vs private: The agent is publicly accepted as confirmed town (sigil strike announced or role claim corroborated) and has no private information about the quiet player, so there is no divergence, and the village's read is unverified.

action: When your sigils are spent or a single one remains and the vote targets a player whose role would be revealed on death, use the day discussion to steer the village toward a vote that preserves the most town value. Ask for night results from the power roles, ask who each candidate visited or was seen by, and push the vote toward the player whom those reports implicate. If the sentinel or the investigator votes against the majority and has real data, weigh that dissent heavily before joining the pile-on. If no evidence separates the candidates, put the cheapest-to-lose candidate first (one without a plausible power-role claim) and keep the remaining sigil for a night when the suspect pool is narrow, so the strike is a guaranteed kill rather than a guess.
situation: Late-game vote among few unconfirmed players. The sigilist is safe and has little or no ability left, and wrongly eliminating a town role is a real risk. The remaining sigil can end the game if the pool is narrowed. Information landscape: Fairly rich on the cleared side (investigator results, healer saves) but without direct evidence against any of the remaining unconfirmed players. Stakes: Close to parity: one wrong vote nearly decides the game, but the revealed role of a miseliminated player can narrow the pool and set up a decisive sigil strike. Consensus: The village is split loosely, aligned on process of elimination among unconfirmed players, with a confirmed role dissenting. My position: with_majority Heat: Virtually zero; cleared by an investigator report or an announced sigil strike. Forward exposure: Speaking up spends little and is easily revised. A vote cannot be taken back. A remaining sigil should not be revealed beyond what is already public, since holding it makes the agent a possible kill target. Target landscape: Three or so unverified players: an exhausted-ability sentinel, a quiet unclaimed player and an active unclaimed player, with only behavior as a basis. Public vs private: Privately the agent knows how many sigils remain and what the sigil result was; publicly the village treats them as town. Private information is consistent with the public read but does not resolve the target.

action: When two players dispute the same role claim and you hold private evidence about one of them, vote according to that evidence. A sigil result of 'no effect' on a claimant only means they did not attack that night, and that is what a Healer, a Town role or any non-attacker produces. So treat it as consistent with a real Healer, never as a mark against them. Before the vote, tally every hard fact: Game Master-announced saves, Trailseer or Sentinel visit reports, and who the claimants' votes protected. Vote for the claimant whose story the corroborated visits contradict, and do not follow the majority against a claimant whose visit a Trailseer or Sentinel report corroborates. If you are the genuine holder of the contested role (e.g. Sigilist, with your own night record to prove it), counter-claim openly and push the vote against the impostor, whose invented action your record exposes.
situation: Day vote with two players claiming the same role (Healer or Sigilist) after a night death or an attack save. Trailseer or Sentinel reports, announced saves and your own sigil result offer partial evidence. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced saves, visit reports from Trailseer or Sentinel, conflicting role claims, and your private sigil outcomes. Stakes: The mid-game board is close. Eliminating a genuine protective Town role strips Town of night protection and sets up the wolves' win. Eliminating a caught impostor, such as the Serial Killer, removes a lone killer and secures Town's lead. Consensus: The room is split or leaning one way, based on conflicting claims and partial visit reports rather than agreed hard proof. My position: Driving the vote when you hold the true role. Otherwise holding out against the majority if the evidence favors the corroborated claimant. Heat: Low to moderate. You may be accused of opportunistic counter-claiming by an evil player, but nothing on the record says you are guilty. Forward exposure: A public vote on one of two role claimants commits you to that person's guilt, and the revealed role at death is permanent and can't be undone. If you vote wrong, you carry the accountability. A true counter-claim of your own role also exposes you to wolf night kills while keeping the sigils unspent. Target landscape: Two claimants for the same role (Healer or Sigilist). One has a visit or story verified by Trailseer or Sentinel reports or announced saves. The other has an unverified or contradicted claim, or was caught at a death scene. The evidence is mechanical, not just behavioral. Public vs private: You privately hold sigil or role knowledge, such as a no-effect sigil result or knowing your own role with certainty. That knowledge either contradicts or backs a public claimant dispute, and a no-effect result does not prove the target is evil.

action: At four alive with no sigils left and a match-point vote, vote for the suspect whom hard evidence ties to evil. Hard evidence means a trailseer sighting at a victim's door, a sigil that failed on a night-immune attacker, a dead investigator's will, or a vote that mirrors a revealed wolf's. Cast the vote early to consolidate the cleared bloc into a three-vote majority. If no hard evidence separates the candidates, break the tie with the voting record against known wolves. Do not pick on a dead player's accusation or on one player's defensiveness alone, because a wrong elimination at parity gives the wolves the game.
situation: Four players alive, with the sigilist's abilities spent and the town facing a win-or-lose vote between unconfirmed survivors. One wolf or a lone killer is among them, and a wrong elimination hands the game to evil. Information landscape: Rich historical evidence: role reveals, wills, voting records, trailseer reports, and what the failed sigils showed. There is often no direct check on which living player is the killer or wolf. Stakes: At four alive with evil one elimination from parity, this single vote decides the game. A correct vote can win it immediately, and a wrong one lets the surviving evil win at night. Consensus: The cleared town bloc is largely aligned and looks to the sigilist as a trusted voice. The only open question is which of the remaining unconfirmed players to eliminate. My position: driving Heat: Near zero. The sigilist is accepted as a confirmed or established town anchor and has cleared itself through a trailseer report or a consistent record. Forward exposure: The vote is public, permanent and irreversible. A correct elimination ends the wolf or killer threat. A wrong one at parity loses to the night kill. Leaving the vote with a slight majority gives no way to recover. Target landscape: Two or three unconfirmed survivors, among them a wolf and a lone killer or neutral. They are separated by evidence (tracking, a sigil failing, a will clearing one player, a voting-record link to a dead wolf) versus mere behavior or a dead player's accusation. Public vs private: With no sigils left there is no private result to add. The vote rests on public evidence: confirmed role reveals, wills, trailseer reports and voting records. In the one case where a failed sigil was known, it matched a public tracking report.

action: Spend a sigil only on a suspect you expect to attack with their own hands that night, such as the likely wolf carrier or a lone killer. First work out who carries the kill: wolves rotate in seat order, so a non-carrier or a Chanteuse/Illusionist doing an ability-only night will not trigger it. If the leading suspect is probably the Serial Killer, expect the sigil to strike nothing, since night immunity stops it. If the suspect is a Necromancer, remember that attacks through a reanimated body are not punished by a sigil. When the morning shows a reanimated attack, put the sigil on a living suspect only as a read check and do not count on a strike. Do not place on investigative or protective roles, which do not attack. Without a concrete attacker hypothesis, hold the remaining sigils.
situation: Mid-game, one or two wolves may be dead and a lone killer (Serial Killer or Necromancer) is still active. The sigilist has to decide whether to commit a sigil on a suspect or hold, with no confirmed knowledge of who will attack tonight. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich from claims, investigator checks, healer saves and trail results. The attacker's identity is unresolved, and the Necromancer or Serial Killer is still hidden. Stakes: The board is close, and each night's kill erodes Town toward the lone killer or wolf parity. A wasted sigil gives up half of the sigilist's lifetime capability, but a well-aimed one can punish an attacker. Forward exposure: Placing is a hidden visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer may see. It permanently spends one of two charges and cannot be undone. The sigil strikes only if the target attacks directly that night, so a non-attacker or a body-channelled attack leaves it wasted. Target landscape: Several unverified players. The leading wolf suspect may be a non-carrier, the claimed investigator, healer or sentinel are role-locked, and a lone killer is among the unknowns. Suspicion rests on behavior and vote history rather than hard evidence.

action: When only the Serial Killer or the wolves' last carrier is left and a single unverified player is the main suspect, put the last sigil on that suspect. A sigil that has no effect on a night when someone else was killed shows the suspect either did not attack or is immune. Combine this with Trailseer or Sentinel results: if the suspect visited the victim and the sigil did nothing, they are probably night-immune, i.e. the Serial Killer. Announce the sigil result and the visit trace the next day so Town can vote the suspect out.
situation: Both wolves are dead, a lone killer remains, and survivors are few. Suspicion has narrowed to one unverified player. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed wolf deaths, a healer save, tracked visits and role claims leave one unresolved suspect. Stakes: With about five alive and a lone killer striking nightly, one more mistake or lost power role could decide the game. Resolving who the killer is wins the game by vote. Forward exposure: Using the final sigil leaves no night actions for the rest of the game. The result must be disclosed publicly to be useful, which reveals the sigilist's role. A visit trace exists, and the placement cannot be reversed. Target landscape: Around five survivors, with the healer, investigator and trailseer role-locked by claims or checks. One unverified player, such as a claimed vigilante, is the only plausible killer.

action: On the opening night, with no deaths, claims, votes or tracker/visit evidence, keep both sigils and place none. A blind sigil only strikes if the target attacks that night. Of the 10 players, only the wolf carrier and possibly the serial killer attack at all, so a random pick usually returns 'no effect' and burns a charge, as in the first-night cases where the target did nothing or only investigated. Hold until a concrete lead exists: a night death pattern, a pushed suspect, or a claimed role contradicted by results. Then place the sigil on the player most likely to carry the kill.
situation: Night 1, discussion-only Day 1 behind you, ten players alive and no information. You must choose between spending one of two sigils on a speculative target and holding both for an evidence-backed night. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths, claims, votes or visit records to separate attackers from passive town roles. Stakes: Early game with no pressure. Parity is far off and nothing is at stake tonight, so the only real cost is the charge, and holding it costs nothing. Eight of the nine possible targets are unlikely to attack tonight. Forward exposure: Holding reveals nothing and is fully reversible, so both charges stay available. Placing a sigil is a visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer can log, and it spends the charge permanently whether or not it triggers. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unvetted. There are no role claims, voting history or night results, so any target pick is a guess among mostly non-attacking roles.

action: From Night 2 on, when a killer is evidently active and you have a lead, place a sigil on the player most likely to be the night's attacker. Rank candidates by what the board shows: who the night deaths and attack types point toward, whose claims Sentinel or Trailseer results contradict, and who the town is pushing in votes. Pick quiet or silent players only on mechanical evidence, not because they are quiet. After the night, treat 'no effect' as ambiguous. It means only that the target did not attack, or was protected or immune. It does not clear the target or confirm them as evil, and you should not defend or accuse on that basis. Keep the last charge for a better lead.
situation: Post-abstain or split-vote Night 2 or later, with a wolf pack and a lone killer both possibly active. You have both sigils and some behavioral leads but nothing confirmed. Information landscape: Mostly info-starved. There are partial claims, a split vote record and perhaps a first-night death, but no confirmed alignments. Stakes: Two killing factions are active and each night costs Town a player, so a successful strike could remove a killer. A miss leaves you with a single charge and a visit on record. Forward exposure: The sigil is a hidden visit that is only visible if a tracker or Sentinel logs it, or if you strike and the death is announced. The charge is spent for good. A 'no effect' result gives you no hard read, so do not build later claims or defenses on it. Target landscape: Players pushed in the Day 2 vote, the players pushing them, claimed info roles, and quiet unread players. Evidence is mostly behavioral. Evil players who use a non-attack ability (investigating, blocking) can look just like innocents on a 'no effect' result.

action: Spend the last sigil on a suspect only when two things hold. First, the suspect is a wolf by strong evidence, such as a tracker-caught visit combined with a deflecting claim and a lone vote against the tracker. Second, the wolf kill rotation (carrier moves through living wolves in seat order, using which wolf carried earlier kills) makes it plausible that this suspect carries tonight's kill. The sigil only strikes if the target attacks that night. Pick the wolf whose carrier turn is due, not simply the most suspicious voter. If the rotation points to the suspect's partner, or the suspect is not a wolf, keep the sigil for a later night.
situation: Late midgame, one sigil left. The town has claimed tracker or sentinel information and a suspect has emerged from vote or tracking anomalies. The sigilist must decide whether to gamble the final sigil on a night-attack trigger. Information landscape: Information-rich. There are public role claims, tracker and sentinel reports, announced deaths and a public voting record, but no confirmed wolf identity and no knowledge of who carries tonight's kill. Stakes: Wolves are within a couple of eliminations of parity, and a lone killer may still be alive. A sigil kill on a carrier wolf would remove a wolf immediately and confirm the sigilist. A miss burns the last tool and leaves the role without night action. Forward exposure: Placing the sigil is a private visit that could be seen by a sentinel or trailseer. The sigil is spent whether or not it triggers, so it is irreversible. A strike would be announced as a sigil kill and would reveal the sigilist. A no-effect result tells nothing, because it looks the same whether the target did not attack, was protected, or was immune. Target landscape: A few behavioral suspects stand out, such as the lone voter against a claimed trailseer or a player caught visiting another by the tracker. Roles are unverified and the evidence is behavioral. Each suspect only matters if they carry the wolf kill that night.

action: Keep the last sigil unspent when the only basis for a target is that they visited a door, or that they have not made a protective claim. A visitor may be the healer, sentinel or trailseer rather than an attacker, and a sigil on a non-attacker does nothing. Wait until the suspect has a trait that makes them likely to attack tonight. Examples: they are a confirmed or near-certain wolf whose carrier turn is due, or earlier night results point to them as an attacker. Until then, use the unspent sigil as a deterrent and as a way to confirm yourself later.
situation: Players are confirmed to have visited a victim or a claimed investigator's door, and the sigilist is tempted to sigil the unclaimed visitor as the presumed attacker. Visiting does not imply attacking, since a healer's protective visit looks the same. Information landscape: Information-rich on who visited, but weak on who attacked. Visit lists and claims exist, and nothing distinguishes a protective visit from an attack. Stakes: The sigil is the last deterrent. Wasting it on a protective role leaves town with no reactive kill and no way to catch a carrier wolf at night. Holding costs little at this distance from parity. Forward exposure: Holding commits nothing and reveals nothing, and the sigil can still be placed on a later night. Spending it on a visitor wastes it permanently and gives no information, because a no-effect result cannot show whether the target was innocent. Target landscape: Two or more players are known to have visited a door. One has claimed a protective role and the other has not. Claim status is the only distinguishing evidence, which is thin and easily misread. The unclaimed visitor could be the real healer, or the real attacker.

action: With a sigil left and a read on who is likely carrying the kill, place it on the most probable killer, then disclose the outcome truthfully in the next day's discussion. If it strikes, the announced sigil death names the wolf. If it has no effect, treat that as a data point (target did not attack, or was shielded), and pair it with other confirmed reads such as an investigator's Suspicious result to push a vote on the player you suspect. Don't sit on the sigil: an unplaced sigil expires with you and gives neither a strike nor a read.
situation: Mid-game with a sigil still available, thin evidence, and a village that abstained or split. Wolves still rotate the kill and the sigilist is trying to convert a suspicion into a strike or a usable data point. Information landscape: Info-starved to moderate: a single day-two vote record, an unverified investigator claim, and no confirmed wolf identities. The carrier cannot be known in advance, so behavioral suspicion is the only basis. Stakes: The board is not yet at parity, so there is room for a speculative placement. A miss costs only a sigil, while a hit removes a wolf outright, and the disclosure can still help the village converge. Forward exposure: Placing the sigil is a secret visit and reveals nothing unless the target attacks. It cannot be undone once placed. Disclosing a failed sigil in daytime reveals your role, but it can be used to back a consensus vote. Target landscape: Players with outlier or aggressive votes, players an investigator has flagged or cleared, and the passive abstainers. Evidence is mostly behavioral, plus one reported check. Wolves rotate the carrier, so a wolf target may not be the one attacking that night.

action: When named as a quiet unknown in a 4-player endgame with the Speculator's pick on Town and the confirmed information (a dead Investigator's will, dead killers) still unresolved, answer promptly instead of withholding. Endorse any posthumous clearances that are announced facts and ground your case in public voting records. Point to the specific vote or claim of the other unconfirmed player that contradicts that confirmed info. If your read of them is sincere, steer the cleared Town players toward a single vote on that player. This makes the Town-pick win the aligned outcome.
situation: Late-game endgame after the lone killer and one wolf are dead and the Investigator has died with a revealed will. Town must find the final wolf, and the Speculator's Town pick depends on that vote. The Speculator is pressured as a silent unknown. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed wills, dead roles, announced eliminations and a complete public voting history are available to cite. Stakes: With four alive and one wolf left, one wrong vote lets the wolf reach parity, so the vote decides the game and the Speculator's Town pick. Consensus: The room is split between two suspects but is receptive to evidence. Cleared players are weighing the voting records and claims to decide who is the last wolf. My position: Driving the discussion, actively shaping which of two suspects gets the vote. Heat: High: two or more players have explicitly named you as the quiet unknown who stayed under the radar all game. Target landscape: Binary choice in a 4-player endgame between yourself (quiet, no claims) and one unconfirmed player who claims Town on a weak basis such as a non-triggering sigil. The other living players are cleared or semi-confirmed Town. The evidence is a confirmed will, dead role reveals and public vote history, not just behavior.

action: When a claimed Town power role demands your role in a late-game, evidence-rich endgame, do not stonewall for the whole game. Give a short, credible answer, ideally revealing your neutral Speculator identity and your Town pick, since the pick was already announced. Then redirect to the hard contradiction between claims. Before pushing any execution, check whether the contradiction could be an honest misunderstanding of the rules. For example, a Sentinel's watch is a visit but is not shown in its own result, so a Trailseer log and a Sentinel report can conflict honestly. If so, argue for voting on the player whose story is contradicted by announced facts, not on a rules slip.
situation: With one wolf left, the claimed Vigilante demands the Speculator's role while the claimed Trailseer and Sentinel accuse each other over contradictory logs. Stonewalling and branding the Sentinel on a mechanics slip got a true Town player executed and exposed the Speculator to a night shot. Information landscape: Information-rich on paper (confirmed dead roles, a direct log contradiction), but the contradiction is open to an innocent mechanics explanation. Stakes: At four alive with one wolf left, a Town misvote lets the wolf win, and it defeats the Speculator's Town pick. Refusing to claim also invites a night shot. Consensus: The room is fractured over conflicting tracking logs, and the credible Vigilante is steering it toward whoever looks mechanically inconsistent. My position: Driving a vote, but only by deflecting onto a rules-confusion rather than proven deceit. Heat: High: a credible claimed Vigilante named you as the primary Illusionist suspect for withholding your role all game. Target landscape: Three candidates in a 4-player endgame: the claimed Sentinel, the claimed Trailseer, and yourself under pressure from a claimed Vigilante whose shot gave them credibility. The claims conflict on mechanics. The evidence is mixed: some mechanical, some behavioral.

action: When the room is arguing over the Day 2 vote record or other public facts and a player misstates them, correct the record in neutral, factual terms (who voted for whom, what the Game Master announced). Keep your own reads low-profile. Do not add speculative doubt about a claimed Investigator or other town information source that the room is leaning on. If you do doubt them, save it until you have concrete evidence, such as a contradiction in the vote record. Your win depends on the side you pick, so keep Town's information bloc coherent and your own heat low until you have picked.
situation: Day discussion after night deaths. The room is sorting suspects using Day 2 votes and a claimed investigator's check, and someone misstates the record or the town is tempted to split over trust in the claimed investigator. The Speculator has not yet picked, or is about to pick Town. Information landscape: Moderately to highly info-rich: confirmed dead wolf roles, concealed bodies, a public vote history, and an unverified investigator claim. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions (wolves plus a lone killer) still alive. A town mis-elimination here helps the killers and can cost the speculator its pick. Preserving town cohesion and accurate information matters more than scoring a read. Consensus: Loosely aligned around the public voting record and the claimed investigator's check. The room is fragile and vulnerable to misremembered facts or manufactured rifts. My position: With the majority, contributing facts rather than driving a vote. Heat: None to low: not accused, seen as a neutral contributor. Target landscape: Several unconfirmed players (a quiet player, a player who voted against a now-dead player, a player cleared by an unverified investigator claim), with dead confirmed wolves and concealed bodies. Suspicion rests on vote records, which are checkable, and on unverified claims.

action: When a claim conflict (dueling investigators, rival healers, or a suspicious door-traffic report) dominates the room and nobody is suspicious of you, stay out of the dispute and anchor on game-master-confirmed facts (announced saves, revealed roles, mechanics such as what a roleblock implies). Make short, neutral, mechanics-based remarks that sharpen the contradiction without backing either claimant. Let the room spend its attention on the claim fight. While you stay unpressured, watch which side's claims hold up against announced facts, and use that to time your side pick: lock in Town when town's information clearly dominates, and wait if the picture is still murky.
situation: Day discussion after a night with an announced save or attack. Rival claimants or an unverified night-result report have triggered a claim duel, and the speculator is an uninvolved bystander who has not yet picked a side. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: a public announcement of a save or death, confirmed roles, and several claimed night results that can be cross-checked, though most claims remain unverified. Stakes: Mid-game with the board not yet at parity. A single vote is not decisive, but a wrong early read or being pulled into the fight would put a speculator that has not yet picked at risk of dying and losing. Staying alive and keeping a flexible pick matter most. Consensus: The village is forming around resolving the claim contradiction, using announced night results as the basis. It has not settled on a single target, and attention sits on the claimants rather than on quiet players. My position: With the emerging majority, holding a neutral, grounding posture without driving any accusation. Heat: None. No one has voiced suspicion of the speculator, and an early innocent check or lack of notice keeps it out of focus. Target landscape: Two or more competing claimants (investigator vs investigator, healer vs healer, or an unprompted door-visit reporter accused of being a necromancer) with some announced facts (a saved player, a dead sentinel) to test them against. The speculator is not among the candidates and has no suspicion on it.

action: At four alive with one wolf left and you have picked Town, first list who is verified by announced facts (revealed roles, read-out wills, confirmed kills). Then vote for the one player no announced fact clears, and vote together with the verified Town players. Ignore that player's counter-accusation against you unless it cites an announced fact. A correct vote here ends the game as a Town win, which is also your win. If two unverified players remain besides you, pick the one whose claims or votes conflict with announced facts.
situation: Four alive after the Investigator's death. The Serial Killer or Necromancer is already gone. One wolf remains, and the village must eliminate it today or lose to a night kill. The agent has already picked Town. Information landscape: Information-rich. The Investigator's will clears a player, spent abilities are logged, and the lone killer's elimination is confirmed. Only one player stays unverified. Stakes: One wrong lynch leaves three alive, and a night kill then gives the wolf parity and the win. A correct lynch ends the game as a Town win and pays out the Speculator's pick. This vote decides the game. Consensus: Verified Town players agree the last wolf must go now, or the night brings parity. They are split only on which unverified player it is, and they reason from wills and role reveals. My position: With the majority, casting the deciding vote alongside the verified Town players. Heat: Exposed. The suspect openly pushes to eliminate the agent, citing a quiet record. This is behavioral, with no hard evidence against the agent. Target landscape: Two unverified players, the agent and one suspect, among four survivors. The other two are cleared by wills or roles revealed through announcements. The suspect has survived earlier scrutiny and now pushes the agent as a binary choice. The basis is announced evidence, not tone.

action: When two claimed roles contradict each other at four alive, check each claim against the game rules and announced facts before voting. A claimant misstating a rule, such as saying a watch is not a visit, is a slip and does not prove they are a wolf. Weigh which claim is consistent with announced facts and who gains if it is false. Vote for the player whose story is contradicted by announced facts or by the rules. If neither story can be settled, vote for the player who has avoided commitment or whom no announcement supports. Do not follow a claimed Vigilante's push on one rules slip alone. A wrong vote at four alive leaves three and a likely loss.
situation: Four alive with one wolf left and the lone killer dead. A claimed Sentinel and a claimed Trailseer contradict each other over whether watching is a visit. The Vigilante pushes to eliminate the Sentinel, and the agent joins. Information landscape: Information-rich on past deaths: the lone killer is dead and wills are public. The decisive contradiction is unverified claim against claim. Mechanics and announced facts are the only tie-breakers. Stakes: Lynching a real Town role at four alive leaves three players. The wolf then kills at night for parity and a win, and the Speculator's Town pick fails. The vote has no margin for error. Consensus: The room follows the Vigilante's push on a single rules-based contradiction. They have not tested it against the rules or looked for an alternative explanation. My position: With the majority, joining a vote to lynch a claimed role. The agent is following the consensus and has not formed an independent read. Heat: High. A claimed Vigilante accuses the agent of hiding their role and dodging deduction. The vote then shifts to another target, so the pressure is behavioral. Target landscape: A claimed Sentinel versus a claimed Trailseer with contradictory night-action claims, plus the unclaimed agent under pressure. Neither claim is confirmed by an announcement. The accusation rests on a rule interpretation, not on evidence.

action: When a late-game wagon forms on you at about four alive, defend with verifiable facts instead of only counter-accusing. Say you are the Speculator, whose pick was publicly announced as Town, so your win depends on Town winning and you have no reason to protect a wolf or the killer. Then rebut the accuser's evidence point by point; one dead player's earlier vote is a weak basis for a lynch. Point to the hard evidence against the real remaining evil: confirmed wills, a trailseer or investigator result, or voting alignment with dead wolves. Ask the others to hold one day on you and test your read. If the wagon still cannot be turned, shift your vote to the most likely evil player in the room rather than standing alone.
situation: Four players are alive and a last evil player remains. The room unites to lynch the Speculator over a dead player's past vote, while the Speculator pushes a lone counter-vote on the real evil player. If the Speculator is lynched, the evil side reaches parity the next night and Town loses. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths and wills, full public voting histories, and visit reports clearing some players. The accusation against you rests on interpretation of that evidence, not on a role check. Stakes: Losing you at four alive leaves too few Town players to survive the night kill, so the lynch decides the game. Winning your Town pick requires staying alive or pulling the vote onto the last evil player. Consensus: Near-unanimous against you, anchored on a single piece of voting-record evidence that the surviving evil player keeps amplifying. My position: Holding out alone against a unanimous counter-wagon. Heat: Severe. The room is treating a dead player's earlier vote against you as definitive proof. Target landscape: The surviving evil player, tied to dead wolves by voting history, versus yourself, accused on a dead player's earlier vote. Everyone else is a confirmed or presumed Town claimant. The evidence on both sides is a mix of records and behavior.

action: At match point with a lone killer or last wolf alive, do not cast an isolated vote that cannot change the result. Before voting, count the votes. If a wagon is already two votes strong on someone you cannot clear, vote with it when your read gives no better target. If you are convinced the wagon is wrong, pitch your target to a second voter or try to force a tie so nobody is eliminated, rather than splitting off alone. Choose the vote that keeps the most Town-aligned players alive into the next night. Say your reasoning publicly before the vote.
situation: Four are alive with both wolves dead and only a killer left. The village is at match point. The Speculator splits off from the wagon on a different player, and the lone vote gets no support and draws a retaliatory vote on the Speculator. The wrong player is eliminated and the killer closes out the game. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves are confirmed dead, the investigator has revealed all of its checks, and the previous day's voting records are fully established. The unresolved question is which of the last three is the killer. Stakes: One mistaken lynch at four alive lets the killer finish within a night or two. Every vote counts, and an isolated vote wastes a Town-aligned vote. Consensus: Split, with a wagon forming on one player led by a claimed investigator. You are the only voter on a different target. My position: Holding out on a lone vote against the forming wagon. Heat: Moderate. A suspect accused you of deflecting and aimed their vote at you. Target landscape: The quiet suspect already under a wagon, the player who dodged the earlier vote on a dead wolf, and a claimed investigator steering the wagon. Roles are claimed but unverified, and the basis is mixed record and behavior.

action: After picking the side you expect to win (Town, in both cases here), use your vote as the swing in a split day vote. Pick the unconfirmed, behaviorally suspicious candidate over confirmed or claimed protective Town roles (healer, vigilante, investigator). If the room is scattered, join the candidate who already has a plausible block and aim to tie or finish that player off, so no protective Town role is eliminated. Prefer a vote that eliminates a likely killer (a quiet player with a suspect vote history, or one who contests a Town claim without evidence). If there is no clear target, a tie that denies the wolves a free Town elimination beats a scattered vote.
situation: Mid-game day vote (day 2-4) with a few night kills already made and more than one killing faction possibly alive. The speculator has already privately picked Town or is about to, and Town's survival decides its win. One or two votes decide whether a protective Town role dies or a killer is removed. Information landscape: Moderate: some claims (healer, investigator, trailseer, sigilist results), concealed or revealed deaths, and public vote records. Nothing fully verified, so reads are partly behavioral. Stakes: The board is close to parity with two killing factions, so each elimination matters. Losing a protective Town role or splitting the vote lets the killers gain ground, while removing a killer or forcing a tie that spares a Town role keeps Town ahead and the speculator's pick alive. Consensus: Fragmented or deadlocked: votes are scattered across 3-5 candidates or split between two suspects, with no dominant read, so a few votes decide the outcome. My position: with majority Heat: Low to none; no accusations aimed at the speculator, who has stayed neutral or factual in discussion. Target landscape: Several live candidates: a claimed protective Town role (healer) under pressure, plus unconfirmed players with only behavioral reads (a quiet player, one challenging a Town claim's timeline, one who voted against a now-dead Town role). No hard confirmation on the unconfirmed players; the evidence is claims and vote history.

action: While no evil role has been confirmed eliminated, no healer save or investigator result has been validated, and no faction has a clear lead (Night 1, or Night 2 after only concealed or unclear deaths), hold the pick and do not guess. Keep the choice open and re-evaluate each night. Commit by Night 3, or sooner if the board is tilting toward your own death, because a Speculator that dies unpicked loses. Dying with a pick still wins if the side wins, so do not hold past the point where a night kill on you is likely.
situation: Early night (Night 1 or 2) as an unrevealed Speculator with the one-time irreversible pick still unspent. No faction has shown momentum, and the Speculator is not a visible target. Information landscape: Information-starved: few or no confirmed roles, untested claims, concealed bodies, and no verified investigator or healer results. Stakes: Nothing is decided yet and the pick cannot be changed. Waiting costs little unless the Speculator itself is at risk of dying unpicked, while an early pick locks in a guess before faction strength is visible. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self, plus holding the pick. All players are unvetted or only partly vetted. Deaths so far are concealed, no evil has been eliminated, and every faction still looks viable. Any read is behavioral guesswork.

action: Pick Town on the night right after Town eliminates a system-confirmed evil role (wolf, killer, or illusionist) and the board is info-rich. That means confirmed evil kills, a publicly validated healer save, and a vindicated investigator, with Town holding a clear numerical majority. Before committing, count the remaining threats: the other wolf, an unidentified lone killer, and Town's own mis-vote or mis-shot risk. If exactly one evil faction remains and Town's lead survives losing a couple of members, pick Town now. If Town is thin or visibly misfiring (a vigilante shooting wildly, mislynch momentum), and you are not currently the likely night target, weigh holding one more night to watch the vote. Never delay so long that a night kill can take you unpicked.
situation: Night 3, after a Day 3 vote eliminated a confirmed evil role on the strength of a vindicated investigator claim. The healer's earlier save is confirmed and Town has a large majority. The Speculator must decide whether to spend the irreversible pick now. Information landscape: Information-rich: system-confirmed role reveal of an eliminated evil, a publicly confirmed healer save, and a validated investigator check. One wolf or a lone killer may still be unknown. Stakes: Town is ahead, but the lead can erode through its own mislynches and mis-shots, as two of the observed losses show. The pick is permanent and announced next morning, tying your result to Town's survival. A confirmed evil elimination is the best moment to lock in. The one winning case committed here, and two losing cases show the pick is only as safe as Town's later discipline. Target landscape: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or Self. Town looks dominant after a confirmed evil elimination, with active power roles (investigator, healer, trailseer, sigilist, vigilante) against one or two weakened evil factions. The basis is system-confirmed outcomes, not behavior. The residual risk is Town's own mistakes, such as mis-eliminating its power roles or the vigilante shooting wrongly.

action: When a night-2 or day-2 conflict exists (a disputed claim, a suspicious check, an unexplained death) and you hold a private, truthful Trailseer result or roleblock record, disclose it on day 2-3 and tie it to the specific suspect. Branches: (a) if you were roleblocked on consecutive nights, say so, because it proves an active Chanteuse and backs a claimed Investigator's suspicious result; (b) if your follow shows a quiet player visiting a victim whose role was concealed, state it and explain that an Illusionist conceal hides only the carrier's visit, so other visits still show; (c) if a player cites door-traffic knowledge when the Sentinel is dead, ask how they got it, because that points to a Necromancer. Name the suspect and push the room toward a vote on that evidence, and be ready to answer fabrication counter-claims by stating the rules precisely.
situation: Day 2-3 after a night-2 attack, blocked actions, or colliding claims. A wolf, Necromancer, or Chanteuse is hiding among the suspects, and the Trailseer holds private information that can break the deadlock. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed or concealed dead role, announced Healer saves, public voting records, and claimed check or visit logs that can be cross-checked. Stakes: Mid-game with several players still alive. One correct elimination of a wolf or the Necromancer removes a key evil ability and shifts the balance, while a wrong vote costs town its margin. Consensus: The town is unsettled or split over a mechanical question (what the concealment hides, whether one claim is impossible). It is receptive to a clear, evidence-based explanation, and it votes together once the mechanics are resolved. My position: Driving the accusation or interrogation, often alongside a confirmed or consistent Investigator or Healer. Heat: Low to moderate. Often none, because you are seen as a helpful, rule-clear voice. Heat rises to moderate when the accused counter-accuses you of faking the claim. Forward exposure: Revealing the Trailseer role or a roleblock history marks you as a likely target for the night kill or the Chanteuse's block. The reveal is irreversible, but it builds credibility when the evidence is checkable and the claim fits other results. Target landscape: A quiet or vocal suspect who defended a dead wolf, was seen at the victim's door, claimed impossible information, or contradicted a verified claimant, versus counter-accused claimants and cautious players waiting for more proof. The basis is the follow log or mechanical contradiction, not mood. Public vs private: Privately hold a follow result, roleblock notice, or knowledge of the rules that sharpens a public dispute. Publicly the town is confused, split on mechanics, or unsure whom to trust.

action: When two players claim the same unique role, or a claim contradicts the rules, speak early to state the structural fact (only one Investigator exists, the Sentinel is dead). Frame the day as resolving that one contradiction, ask each claimant to detail their checks and visits, and hold the room on that conflict until the false claimant is exposed and voted out. Do not reveal your own role or roleblock history unless it is needed.
situation: A direct role collision, with two claimants for a single-copy role or a claim that is mechanically impossible, appears on day 2-3 and risks being buried under side topics. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced Healer saves, deaths and revealed roles, and claimed visit logs that can be tested against the game rules. Stakes: One decisive vote can remove a wolf's counterclaim and its concealment power. Letting a false claimant survive could cost town the investigator line. Consensus: The village is split between two claimants and open to guidance. It unites against the false claimant once the contradiction is made the focus. My position: Driving the debate framing without necessarily naming a target first. Heat: None; trusted as a cross-verified or neutral voice. Forward exposure: Low. Framing the rule contradiction exposes nothing about your role, keeps your night utility private, and can be dropped or deepened later. Target landscape: Two claimants of the same unique role, or a claimant with impossible information, with one real and one likely a wolf or Necromancer. The basis is a logical contradiction, with Healer saves and past results as support. Public vs private: Privately know you were blocked or followed someone, which confirms active evil interference, while the public sees only competing claims and does not know which is real.

action: In a late-game endgame (3-4 alive) when you hold a concrete tracking result that confirms or refutes another player's claim, disclose it in full and use it to take a clear stance. Name which of the remaining candidates the result points toward, and tie the result to the contradiction in the opponent's story. For example, if you followed a player who visited no one, that player cannot have made the attack the opponent alleges. Then ask the swing player to confirm what they can from their own side, such as spent sigils or their own claimed visits. Do not stop at sharing the fact and staying neutral on the remaining candidates. Pair the result with a clear vote recommendation and with the public voting record, so the swing voter has something to act on.
situation: Endgame day with 3-4 players alive and one or two evil players left. A claimant is attacking the trailseer's credibility or pushing a narrative that your private tracking result contradicts. The swing voter's vote decides the game. Information landscape: Information-rich: night deaths and roles are revealed, claims are all out, voting records are public, and the trailseer holds a precise follow result that bears directly on the dispute. Stakes: One vote or one more night kill decides the game. A wrong or passive day leads straight to parity or an evil win, so a stance backed by hard evidence is required. Consensus: Split and unsettled at the final stage. No majority has formed, and the swing voter is deciding between two competing narratives. My position: Driving: lead the case with the tracking evidence and an explicit vote call. Heat: Moderate to high. A rival claimant is accusing you of fabricating your reports, or the room is waiting to see which side you take. Forward exposure: Sharing your result and naming a target commits you to a win-or-lose confrontation with the opponent, and it is not reversible. It also exposes your role and the follow target to the wolf. At 3-4 alive the board has no slack, so the commitment is worth making, and withholding a stance costs more than the exposure. Target landscape: Two or three remaining candidates, all with claimed or revealed roles. One is a claimed sentinel or similar who is attacking you or deflecting. One is a swing voter whose own claim your result can corroborate. The basis is hard tracking evidence and public voting history, not tone. Public vs private: You privately know a specific player made zero visits on the key night. This contradicts or confirms what another claimant publicly asserts about who could have made the attack, and the room has not yet drawn the conclusion.

action: When one wolf or killer remains and the other players are arguing over past votes and kill reads, evaluate the voting record yourself instead of dismissing the argument. Identify who voted alongside the already-revealed evil player and who voted against the true protective roles. State which of the candidates the record implicates. Pair it with your tracking fact so you are not seen as neutral. Prevent the surviving evil player from steering the room onto a town-aligned player by anchoring the vote on the public record.
situation: Parity-edge endgame (about 4 alive, one wolf left) where the remaining players argue over past voting records versus a dead role's suspicions. The trailseer is trusted but uncommitted, and a mislynch loses the game. Information landscape: Information-rich in public records (graveyard roles, full voting logs), but without a decisive private proof on the final candidates. Stakes: At 4 alive with a wolf remaining, a wrong day vote makes the next night kill reach parity. The trailseer's voice decides which narrative the room follows. Consensus: Divided between two competing narratives, with no one anchoring on the evidence. The surviving wolf is deflecting by citing a dead player's old read. My position: Holding out in a skeptical middle. Must move to anchor the room on the voting record. Heat: None; you are treated as confirmed town with an active investigative role. Forward exposure: Taking a stance on the voting record commits you to a read that can be checked later. It is correctable by the next vote or by later deaths, and staying neutral is more costly at this parity threshold, where a mislynch loses the game. Target landscape: Two or three remaining candidates: one who voted with a revealed wolf earlier and one the dead vigilante or other power role pointed at. The basis is voting record and a deceased player's read, with no hard tracking evidence on either. Public vs private: Your private result clears one player from suspicion, but the public debate turns on voting patterns. You hold no hard proof on the final candidates, so the voting record is the only usable evidence.

action: When your night tracking produced a concrete visit that points at a living suspect (e.g. a dead investigator's last visit went to a player), state the trail openly in day discussion and cast your vote on that suspect. Do not switch to a different, softer target at the vote. If the room is split between the trail-implicated player and a claimed protective role, back the trail-implicated player so the vote concentrates and does not deadlock. If the trail turns out to be a stationary or empty result, say so plainly and weigh the remaining accusations on behavior rather than abstaining by default.
situation: Late-mid game with a wolf still alive. A town information role has just died, the trailseer privately knows where that role's final visit went, and the vote is split between the trail-implicated suspect and a claimed protective role. Information landscape: Information-rich: a public death, a confirmed save, and a private trailseer track giving a hard lead on a living suspect. Stakes: With about seven alive and a wolf alive, each daytime elimination matters. A tie wastes the day's elimination, lets the surviving wolf coordinate a night kill on the outed trailseer, and brings the wolves closer to parity. Consensus: Fragmented. The room is arguing over simultaneous action resolution and roleblock claims, with no agreed target and a likely tie. My position: holding out Heat: Moderate: a surviving wolf publicly challenges the trailseer's credibility and its understanding of how night visits work. Forward exposure: Reporting the trail commits the trailseer to a claim and makes them a night-kill target, but it is already half-exposed once they have spoken. Voting against the trail's own implication contradicts the stated claim and cannot be undone. A tie caused by a split vote wastes the day's elimination and leaves a wolf free to retaliate. Target landscape: Two or three candidates: a player implicated by a trailseer-observed visit (evidence-based, role unconfirmed) versus a claimed town protective role under behavioral suspicion (no hard evidence). Evidence outweighs behavior. Public vs private: The trailseer privately holds a concrete visit result (a dead investigator's last visit to a living suspect) while public debate is distracted by mechanics arguments and suspicion on a claimed protective role.

action: When the room is split across several unconfirmed suspects and your own tracking gave only stationary or empty results, do not drift into a pointless abstain. Compare the candidates on voting records and on who deflected or pushed wagons, then commit your vote to the most behaviorally suspicious one. If you do abstain, publicly state which candidate you find least supported and why, so the abstain still shapes the room instead of just conceding control to a fragmented vote.
situation: Both wolves are eliminated but a lone killer remains. The investigator's checks are spent, and the town splits into competing accusations with no hard leads. Information landscape: Information-starved: investigator checks exhausted, a healer's protection target already outed, and night tracking returned only stationary results. Stakes: A fragmented plurality can eliminate a town power role (here the vigilante) on a few votes. With a lone killer left, every wrong elimination hurts town, so an abstain that leaves the tally fragmented risks a bad outcome. Consensus: Fragmented: competing accusations against multiple unconfirmed suspects with no shared evidence base. My position: holding out Heat: Low: the trailseer is seen as a trusted town asset after supporting the investigator's mechanics. Forward exposure: A bare abstain is reversible and low-cost to credibility, but it concedes vote control to a fragmented room, where a wrong elimination (even of a town power role) can result. A reasoned vote commits you to a read on the record. Target landscape: Several unconfirmed players (a quiet one, one deflecting onto others, one reserved and claiming no role), none with hard investigative evidence against them, so the choice rests on behavior only. Public vs private: The trailseer privately has only a stationary or empty tracking result that gives no usable information on the remaining evil, and publicly looks like a trusted town asset.

action: In a late-game kingmaker vote (3-4 players alive, one hostile left), cast your vote against the player your own night tracking implicates or fails to clear. Check which accused player's tracked night behavior (visit to the night's victim, or a stationary night matching their claim) agrees with their story, and which contradicts it. If your trace caught one candidate at the murder victim's door, or cleared the other candidate's claim, vote the implicated one and say your trace result plainly, so the remaining town votes with you. Do not let a counter-accusation against your own tracking sway you. Your first-hand trace outranks their framing, and the role pool left by public death records should corroborate it.
situation: Final 3-4 players, wolves mostly or entirely dead, one lone killer (serial killer or necromancer) still alive and pushing a counter-claim or accusation against the trailseer; the trailseer's private trace decides the vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: public death records narrow the possible roles, and the trailseer's night trace of the suspect's visits (or lack of visits) can be checked against claims. Stakes: One vote ends the game either way: eliminating the last hostile wins for town, while a miss gives the killer or wolves parity or a final-round win. Use all the trace evidence you hold. Consensus: A small village near the endgame, split between the accused's counter-narrative and the trailseer's trace-backed case. It is not yet unified, and the trailseer's vote and statement can decide it. My position: driving Heat: Moderate: the suspected killer is counter-accusing the trailseer (retaliatory votes, claims that passive tracking results are fabricated or prove necromancer), but the rest of the room is not convinced by it. Forward exposure: The vote is public, permanent and game-deciding. A correct elimination wins immediately; a wrong one leaves parity or a loss. Stating your trace reveals you as trailseer, but at this stage that costs little against a decisive, verifiable case. Target landscape: Two or fewer candidates, usually a claimed role (sentinel or vigilante) who is pressuring the trailseer versus a claimed role whose stationary or visiting night matches your private trace. Evidence is a first-hand trace plus role-pool elimination from public death records, not mere behavior. Public vs private: Your private trace either caught the accused visiting the victim or cleared the other candidate, matching the public role-elimination logic. It confirms the case against the accused and contradicts their counter-accusation.

action: On a day-2 vote where the room is leaning toward abstaining and you have only one night of tracking data with no hard evidence of guilt, vote to abstain with the majority rather than pushing a solo elimination on the player you followed. Use the day to publicly state your trail result plainly and consistently. Keep following the same suspect, or a new unverified one, that night to gather a second data point. Do this if the followed player's contradictions are only stumbles over rules, or if their claim is unverified. Switch to a vote against them only once a second trail or a hard contradiction (a caught lie, a confirmed role) backs it up.
situation: Day 2 after a night with a death or a concealed body. The trailseer has publicly reported a trail result. The followed player counter-claims or disputes it and votes against the trailseer, while the rest of the town leans toward no elimination. Information landscape: Mostly claims and night-action reports: an unverified counter-claim, a failed or struck sigil, a dead sentinel or healer, a concealed body, and a trail result. Little verified evidence, so a second night of data has high value. Stakes: Mid-game with several wolves and a lone killer still alive. A wrong elimination costs Town real parity margin, while one no-elimination day costs little. The vote is not a swing, so waiting for a second night of data is cheap. Consensus: The village is strongly aligned toward abstaining (about eight of ten) because no hard evidence points to anyone. The alignment rests on caution and lack of information, not on a shared suspect. My position: with majority Heat: Low overall from the room. The followed player may cast a lone retaliatory vote against you, and one or two others may question your tracking report. That is not enough to threaten you. Forward exposure: Abstaining is reversible and low-commitment: it spends no vote on a possibly wrong target and keeps you aligned with the room. The earlier trailseer claim is already public and cannot be undone, so you stay a night-kill target whichever way you vote. A solo elimination vote would add a second visible commitment to an unproven read. Target landscape: The only individual under scrutiny is the player you followed, who gave a contradictory or fumbled counter-claim. There are no confirmed evil players. The basis is behavior and your private trail, not verified evidence. The rest of the room prefers waiting. Public vs private: Privately hold a night-one trail result (the followed player visited someone or no one). Publicly the followed player disputes or reframes it and counter-claims. Nothing is verified, so the alignment of the followed player is unresolved.

action: Pick your follow target by who is most likely to be visiting a night-kill victim. If a role has just been confirmed (a wolf voted out, or the investigator validated and now a prime wolf target), follow either the player most tied to the exposed wolf (defender, lone dissenter, silent suspect) or the endangered information role you expect the wolves to hit. If the followed player visits the night's victim, report it the next day as testimony to vote on. If you are blocked on that target, report that too, since a repeat block on one target also points to the chanteuse. If the endangered role dies, your report of whom they visited gives the town a lead. This works best when the target is a behavioral suspect or likely kill victim, not an arbitrary quiet player.
situation: Mid-game after a wolf flip or after a night kill or save, when the town has some confirmed roles and the wolves are likely to strike a known information role. You choose whom to follow, hoping to see a visit to the night's victim or a pack member's movement. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed wolf, claimed night visits, public roleblock claims, and voting records, though most players' roles are still unverified. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several evils alive. One accurate visit report can identify a wolf and swing the next vote, but a wasted or blocked follow costs a night of intel. Target landscape: Players tied to a confirmed wolf (the defender, lone dissenter, or silent suspect) and the town information role most likely to be killed tonight, versus quiet unvetted players with no evidence against them. Roles are partly revealed through claims and flips; the basis is evidence plus behavior.

action: If you have publicly reported your track and a claimed rival (such as a counter-claiming investigator) has attacked or voted against you, you are the likely wolf target and a follow on that rival is likely to be blocked. Choose a follow target who is not the one hunting you: a suspect from the day's evidence or a plausible kill victim. That way the follow can yield a result even if you are blocked or killed. Report your result openly on the next day.
situation: You have publicly reported a track and a rival counter-claimant has singled you out, so you are the likely wolf kill or block target tonight. Information landscape: Information-rich but disputed: a revealed dead role, conflicting night-visit claims, and an investigator claim that contradicts yours. Stakes: You are probably the wolves' target tonight. If you are blocked or killed with a concealed body, the town gets nothing from your night. Target landscape: The hostile counter-claimant who voted against you, versus other unvetted or quiet players and plausible kill victims. The claimant's role is disputed; the others are unclaimed, and the basis is behavior.

action: On the opening night with no claims or reads, follow one unread player and note whom they visit. On Day 2, report the result accurately and early, with the exact visit or no-visit, and use it to test the room. If the target visited someone, compare it with any claimed Sentinel or Investigator results and with that player's own story, and challenge a target whose claimed role does not fit the visit. If the target visited no one, treat that only as weak evidence that the target did not carry a kill. A hidden-role kill can mask the carrier's visit, so do not clear the target outright. Prefer a target whose visit you can cross-check with other town roles.
situation: Opening night after a discussion-only Day 1, with all ten players alive and no deaths, votes, or claims. The Trailseer must pick a first follow target blind, and the result is the only hard information it will have. Visits can be cross-checked against Sentinel or Investigator claims, and a Night 1 kill may hide the carrier's trace. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are no claims, no voting record, and no night history, only generic Day 1 chatter. The follow result will be the first concrete evidence in the game. Stakes: Early game with a large margin and no single decision deciding the game. The value is in building a verifiable information baseline before wagons form. The Trailseer's own survival matters, since a Night 1 death loses the result and lets a wolf fake-claim the role. Target landscape: Nine unvetted living players with no public claims, votes, or behavioral deviations. The choice is arbitrary and rests on neutral behavioral impressions only. No hard evidence separates wolves, the lone killer, neutrals, or town.

action: When few suspects remain and the board is information-rich, follow the suspect whose claimed role implies a night action that would make them a visible killer (e.g. a claimed vigilante who says they hold their shots). If they visit someone and that person is announced dead by a killer that morning, report the trace publicly and push the vote on that player. If they visit no one, treat that only as a weak clearing of that night. It does not clear the player of being a wolf, because only the carrier visits for the kill. Follow the player whose claim is least verified and who would be the hidden killer by elimination, not the one whose behavior merely looks harmless.
situation: Late game with most evil already eliminated or exposed (wolf corpses revealed, a vigilante or vote having removed one wolf). The town hunts the last remaining killer (final wolf or lone Serial Killer) among a few suspects, and the trailseer must choose whom to follow tonight. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed dead roles, clear public voting records, claimed power roles, and a recent death or save pattern to cross-check a trailseer trace against. Stakes: With about five alive and one killer left, one wrong vote or one more night kill can hand the game to evil or the lone killer. The trailseer's trace may be the only hard evidence that decides the next day's vote. Target landscape: A small set of 2-3 remaining suspects, mostly claimed power roles (vigilante, sigilist) that are unverified, plus quiet players whose votes aligned with dead evil players. Basis is mixed: voting records and corpse reveals narrow the field, but claims are unconfirmed.

action: When you hold 2 bullets, sit at low heat, and the room is hunting among unchecked or shaky-claiming players, don't build the case around one behavioral stumble or a quiet abstainer and then drive the room to a unanimous vote on it. Ask the suspect a concrete question and compare the answer against the game rules. Check whether the 'inconsistency' is a plausible rule-based explanation, for example a sigilist's sigil showing no effect, or a roleblock versus no action. Voice your suspicion as a tentative read, not a certainty, and keep the case reversible. If the suspect's answers fit the rules, or the only evidence is behavior, move the accusation to a better-supported target. Keep your shots in reserve for a night target backed by hard evidence, such as investigator or sentinel results, caught lies, or role-claim contradictions.
situation: Midgame, after one or two deaths (a wolf or other evil already removed, maybe a protective Town role lost). The village debates a claimed Town role's inconsistent explanation or a conspicuous abstainer, and I, the vigilante with 2 bullets, drive the accusation from low heat. Information landscape: Mixed, with partial confirmed roles from deaths and some investigator or sentinel results, but no hard proof against the target. The suspect's explanation can be read in more than one rule-consistent way, so the evidence is behavioral and ambiguous. Stakes: With wolves and a lone killer or neutral still alive, each day vote is costly. Wrongly eliminating a Town power role shrinks Town toward parity and wastes a day without removing evil, so a bad lynch on soft evidence can decide the game. Consensus: The room is open and moves easily behind whoever makes the most coherent case. It is anchored by recent deaths and any sentinel or investigator information, but not yet fixed on a hard-evidence target. My position: driving Heat: Low. The village sees me as a constructive voice and nobody suspects me. Forward exposure: Driving a public accusation commits my credibility to the target's guilt. The village may follow me into a unanimous vote that cannot be undone, while my vigilante role and my shots stay hidden. I can reduce the exposure by framing the read as tentative. Target landscape: A claimed role with a shaky or inconsistent explanation, or an abstainer, versus quiet unchecked players. None has hard investigative clearance or a confirmed wolf link, so the basis is behavioral, not evidentiary. Public vs private: I hold unused vigilante bullets and have no private evidence on any suspect. My accusation rests only on public behavior, so my private knowledge adds no certainty to the public read.

action: When the claimed town roles are cornering the unclaimed players, or a role-call or narrowed suspect pool names you as a candidate, claim vigilante openly in day discussion before the vote. Give your remaining bullet count and the fact that you have held fire, and pair it with a reasoned read on the other unclaimed players. If you are the one cornered, the claim costs little: silence leaves you voted out as the presumed lone killer, with bullets unspent. If the claim is doubted, offer to shoot the player the town agrees on that night, so your role is tested by the night result. Claim early enough that the town can weigh it. A vigilante who dies unclaimed with bullets also gives a necromancer a usable corpse.
situation: Late game with most wolves dead or confirmed. The claimed town bloc is narrowing the hunt for the last wolf or lone killer to a few unclaimed players and demanding role reveals. You are the silent vigilante with bullets in that pool. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are verified by night results, a few evil players are already dead, and investigator clears or sigil results leave only a few unverified candidates. Little ambiguity remains outside that pool. Stakes: The board is small and nearly decided. Losing a confirmed town role with unspent bullets to a day vote is a heavy swing. It can also hand a lone killer (necromancer) a vigilante corpse and tip the game toward the evil side. Consensus: The town is aligned and information-rich. Wolves are mostly dead or the pool is narrowed, and the claimed roles are broadly accepted. The room agrees the remaining evil is among the unclaimed players and is converging on whoever stays quiet. My position: holding_out Heat: High and rising. Claimed town roles are demanding role declarations from unverified players, or an investigator's narrowed pool names you, and non-claiming reads as evasion. Forward exposure: Claiming reveals the vigilante role and the remaining bullet count, so wolves or a killer may target you at night. Silence in a small suspect pool, however, almost guarantees a vote-out with every bullet wasted. A claim is hard to retract. It can be backed up by shooting at night, which also shows the claim is true. Target landscape: A small unclaimed pool: you, a quiet neutral or unverified player, and a possible hidden lone killer or last wolf. The claimed town roles (investigator, healer, trailseer, sigilist, sentinel) are partly verified by night results. The pressure on the pool rests on inactivity and refusal to claim, not on hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the genuine town vigilante with bullets unspent. Publicly you are an unclaimed, quiet player whom the claimed town bloc treats as a likely hiding place for the lone killer or last wolf.

action: When the room is info-rich, with a claimed Town power role corroborated by an announced healer save or a surviving attack, and you hold bullets with zero heat, stay hidden. Add sincere, verifiable support. Confirm any true result about yourself (e.g. 'the investigator cleared me', 'the sigil did nothing on me') and point to the announced night facts that make the claim credible. Then push the village's attention onto the contested player, such as the dissenter, the fake claimant or whoever has impossible knowledge. Do not mention your role, your bullet count, or the fact that you held fire. If the claim is contested, back the claimant whose story fits the announced night report. Spend bullets at night on the wolf or killer the room has already exposed.
situation: A Town power role (investigator or sigilist) has been corroborated by night events and a contested player or counter-claimant is trying to deflect. You are a vigilante with bullets left, already cleared or ignored by the room, in a day discussion with a growing consensus. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced healer saves, dual attack reports, a guilty check, a reported null sigil, visit claims that can be cross-checked against the night report. Stakes: The board is mid-game with a Town lead forming. Keeping the vigilante alive and unrevealed preserves a late-game kill, and an early consensus vote removes a wolf without costing any bullet. Exposure would put the vigilante on the wolves' kill list. Consensus: The village is converging behind the claimed investigator or the evidence-consistent claimant, and the case against the accused is firming up on mechanical facts. My position: With the majority, supporting the forming consensus rather than driving it. Heat: Zero to minimal. Cleared by an investigator result or a null sigil report, and not a suspect for anyone in the room. Forward exposure: Corroborating a Town claim with sincere logic reveals nothing about your role. Claiming vigilante would invite wolf kills and roleblocks and cannot be undone. Staying quiet keeps all options open and can be reversed at any time. Target landscape: A claimed investigator or other Town power role backed by announced evidence, versus a dissenter or counter-claimant whose story contradicts the night report. The basis is hard evidence (announced saves, attack types, consistent results) rather than tone. Public vs private: Privately a vigilante holding live bullets. Publicly an analytical Town voice whose innocence is already attested by a claimed investigator or sigilist, so there is nothing to correct.

action: When your night shot produced a hard, mechanically checkable result (a death the Game Master announced as a vigilante shot, or an 'immune target' notice with no public attack announced), claim vigilante at the start of the day. State exactly what you shot and what you learned: a wolf kill confirmed by the announcement, or 'shot an unverified player without a kill, so they are night-immune, i.e. the Serial Killer'. Then steer the vote or the remaining shot toward the player the result points to. If a bullet remains, say so and ask the healer or the rest of the town to protect you. Expect the accused to call the claim fabricated, and point to the announcements, wills and save history that back it up. The mechanical backing is what makes the claim trusted.
